  namespaced alias, `https://lore.org/claims/root_domains`, for providers that require namespaced
  custom claims. The namespace is a collision-resistant name under a project-controlled domain
  ([RFC 7519](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7519) §4.2), never fetched. The name is fixed rather than configurable, so nothing in an
  attacker-controlled environment response can point the client at a different claim. A static-value claim is plain
  configuration on nearly every surveyed provider: a hardcoded-claim mapper on Keycloak, one
  `setCustomClaim` line in an Auth0 Action, a static custom claim on Okta, a property mapping on
  authentik, an Action on Zitadel.
- **`aud`, where its entries have a usable shape.** An entry that parses as an `https` URI
  contributes its host, and an entry shaped like a domain contributes a suffix, as today. Opaque
  identifiers such as `lore-api` contribute nothing. [RFC 9068](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9068) wants the resource URI in `aud`, so
  P3's static audience does double duty when the operator sets it to the deployment's canonical URL
  or domain, with no extra provider configuration. This rule is also what keeps existing
  `UrcAuthApi` tokens working unchanged: `aud = ["URC", ".epicgames.net"]` yields exactly the
  suffix it does today.

A custom issuer may additionally publish the list in its discovery document, which the client
fetches issuer-verified (D2). Hosted providers cannot extend theirs, so that stays an option for
issuers the deployment controls rather than the baseline.

When neither source yields a domain, the token may be sent only back to the token endpoint it came
from, which the [RFC 8693](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8693) exchange needs, and login fails with a configuration error naming the two
fixes. Failing closed here is the point: defaulting to any server-advertised host would reopen the
hole.

That is deliberately a small change. `store_user_token`
([`lore-credential/src/token_store.rs`](../../lore-credential/src/token_store.rs)) already takes
the domain list as a parameter, so its callers pass this derivation instead of `iss` plus `aud`:
three in
[`lore-revision/src/auth/login.rs`](../../lore-revision/src/auth/login.rs) and two in
[`lore-transport/src/auth/exchange.rs`](../../lore-transport/src/auth/exchange.rs), which also runs
`verify_jwt_usage_for_remote` against the exchanged token before storing it, using the same
derivation. The exchange pair is the Tier 2 path and works by the same rules: an authz token's
`aud` carries the resource URI, whose host is where the token is meant to go, and a provider that
co

entries.title: lore\proposals\2026-08-20-oidc-oauth2-authentication.md
entries.text:
Every claim struct the two crates deserialize into becomes tolerant of a stock provider's output.
On the server `name`, `preferred_username`, `env` and `idp` become `Option`. On the client `name`
becomes optional too, `preferred_username` being optional there already. And
`AuthorizationToken`'s required set narrows to `iss`, `sub`, `aud`, `exp` and `iat`, with
`client_id` read where present.

That is deliberately *less* than the [RFC 9068](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9068) profile, which makes seven claims REQUIRED, adding
`client_id` and `jti`, and whose §4 says a resource server MUST reject a token whose `typ` is not
`at+jwt` or `application/at+jwt`. Requiring the full set would reject the tokens the legacy auth
service issues, which is the one thing phase 1 must not do. So the server requires the five that
every issuer in play already emits, and treats the profile's extras as checks a deployment can turn
on rather than as preconditions. `typ` enforcement is a setting, and `jti` matters only to a
deployment doing replay detection, which is not done today. The list of required fields can be
extended after the legacy deployment support is no longer needed.

Widening also deletes code. `verify_token_internal` decodes `AuthorizationToken`, and on failure
falls back to decoding `JWTUserInfo` and rebuilding an `AuthorizationToken` from it with
`resources: None`. That fallback exists for one reason: `idp` is the only field
`AuthorizationToken` requires that an authentication token does not carry, `resources` and
`groups` being `Option` already. Once every non-registered field is `Option`, `AuthorizationToken`
is a strict superset of `JWTUserInfo` and the second decode is unreachable. The server's
`JWTUserInfo` has no other use, appearing only in that decode and two test helpers, so phase 1
deletes the struct along with the fallback.

This change stands alone. It is small, it is a strict widening, and no token that verifies today
stops verifying. Until it lands, nothing else in this proposal can be tested against a real
provider, so it ships first.

entries.title: lore\proposals\2026-08-20-oidc-oauth2-authentication.md
entries.text:
Two of the custom RPCs ask questions no OAuth 2.0 or OIDC endpoint answers, and they fail the same
way for the same reason. A token carries a grant: neither standard offers a way to *search* the
grant space, or to resolve an identifier that is not the bearer's. Both therefore move off the
authentication path onto optional traits with a degraded default, rather than being forced into a
mechanism that cannot hold them.

#### The user service

`GetUserInfo` resolves a batch of user IDs to display names, and `GetUserId` resolves the reverse.
OIDC has no equivalent, because `/userinfo` describes only the bearer. Nothing in the standard set
replaces these.

The design moves them off the `Authentication` trait onto a separate optional `UserService`
trait. The default implementation answers from the token's own `name` and `preferred_username`
claims for the current user, and returns the raw ID for anyone else. The CLI already degrades to
printing the ID when no name resolves
([`lore-client/src/cli/commands/auth.rs`](../../lore-client/src/cli/commands/auth.rs)), so that
path is exercised today.

Where Lore displays *another* user's name, such as a revision author or a lock holder, the lookup
cannot be avoided. Revision metadata records the user identifier and deliberately not the
name (`created_by` and its siblings in
[`lore-revision/src/revision.rs`](../../lore-revision/src/revision.rs)), so that the identifier can
be unmapped from a person without rewriting history.

The directory lookup therefore stays a real dependency for any deployment that wants names, and
OIDC does not supply one. Deployments with a directory can implement `UserService` over it, SCIM
2.0 being the nearest standard, but out of scope for this change. Deployments without a
`UserService` implementation show identifiers.

The lookup runs on the client and bypasses the Lore server, which keeps personal information out
of it. So the server advertises the directory on the endpoint, and the client picks the
`UserService` implementation from what is advertised:

- `user_url` set: `lore.user.v1.UserService` at `user_url`.
- Otherwise `auth_url` set: the legacy `GetUserInfo` and `GetUserId` RPCs at `auth_url`.
- Neither: the token-only default above.

The directory's host must be under a domain that is found in one of the token's `aud` names.

The directory operations outlive the auth service, so they get gRPC APIs of their own, in the
vocabulary of the other `lore.*.v1` APIs. `lore.user.v1.UserService` has `UserGet` (IDs to users)
and `UserFind` (a username or a display name to users), which the client calls.
`lore.user.v1.RepositoryRegistryService`, served at the same `user_url`, is called by the Lore
server with the caller's token. It has `RepositoryList` (the repositories the caller holds
permissions on), and `RepositoryRegister` and `RepositoryUnregister`, which register the
repositories the server creates and deletes and record the creator as the owner, as `RebacApi`'s
`CreateResource` and `DeleteResource` at `auth_url` do on a `UrcAuthApi` deployment. The server
picks the registry by the same rule: `user_url`, else `auth_url`, else no registration. On every
path the server authorizes the delete before calling the registry: the creator while they can
still reach the repository, or a caller holding `owner` or `admin` on it. The registry may refuse
it too, as `DeleteResource` does for a caller without `admin`. A repeated `RepositoryRegister`
under the same name succeeds, so `ALREADY_EXISTS` means the repository is registered under another
name, and the server refuses the create.

The registry RPCs first shipped on `UserService` as `PartitionList`, `PartitionAdd` and
`PartitionRemove`. Partitions have no names, only repositories do, and the client never calls
them, so they moved to their own service. The old RPCs were deprecated and then removed.

**The user identity is read from the token.** Lore records a user as one string, in `created_by`
and wherever else an identi

entries.title: lore\proposals\2026-08-20-oidc-oauth2-authentication.md
entries.text:
#### Verification and settings [`lore-server/src/auth/jwk.rs`](../../lore-server/src/auth/jwk.rs) needs less work than anything else here. It already fetches a JWKS, caches by `kid`, pins the algorithm to the key rather than the header, bounds the response, throttles refreshes, and recovers from a key rotated under an unchanged `kid`. It gains .well-known discovery-based `jwks_uri` resolution and keeps everything else. The provider is never on the request path. The server calls it at startup and on cache refresh only, and answers every request from the token alone: ```mermaid sequenceDiagram autonumber participant C as Client participant S as Lore server participant P as Identity provider Note over S,P: startup, then cache refreshes only S->>P: GET jwt_issuer/.well-known/openid-configuration P-->>S: jwks_uri S->>P: GET jwks_uri P-->>S: signing keys, cached by kid Note over C,S: every request C->>S: request with access token Note over S: verify signature against cached keys,
check iss, aud, exp,
authorize from permission and resource claims S-->>C: response, with no auth call on the request path ``` Discovery needs no new setting, because `[server.auth]` already names the issuer. `jwt_issuer` is documented as the expected `iss` claim, and under OIDC that is the same string as the discovery issuer: OIDC Discovery §4.3 requires the `issuer` inside the document to equal the URL used as the prefix to fetch it, and [RFC 9068](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9068) §4 requires the resource server to check `iss` against exactly that. So when `jwt_issuer` holds an https URL the server fetches `/.well-known/openid-configuration`, takes `jwks_uri` from it, and goes on comparing `iss` against the same value. `[server.auth.jwk].endpoint` stays as the override for providers with non-standard discovery. A `token_exchange_issuer` that `jwt_issuer` doesn't list is a separate token service with keys of its own. The server discovers them the same way, from ``, and verifies a token whose `iss` names the service against those keys only, and every other token against the `jwt_issuer` keys only, so neither can sign tokens in the other's name. `[server.auth.jwk].endpoint` applies to the `jwt_issuer` keys alone. `[server.auth]` therefore gains `permission_claim`, `implicit_actions`, `baseline_access`, `repository_catalog`, `repository_catalog_url`, `resource_claim`, `resource_id_claim`, `resource_id_template` and `resource_wildcard`. `permission_claim` and `implicit_actions` are exercised from phase 2 onwards, because they are what Tier 1 runs on. `baseline_access` steers only what the default `RepositoryCatalog` lists (D7), never an access decision. The other four only matter once a per-partition claim is in play, so phase 4 for a new deployment and immediately for a `UrcAuthApi` one. There is no service-account setting, because D4 turned that check into two ordinary actions. #### `RepositoryAuthorizer` answers every partition question `RepositoryAuthorizer` changes signature and gains two implementations. The signature changes are needed because D1 made Tier 1 answer every partition question through this trait: ``` struct VerifiedToken<'a> { raw: &'a str, claims: &'a AuthorizationToken } check_repository_access(token: Option<&VerifiedToken>, repository: RepositoryId, action: &str) -> Result<(), Status> ``` Two changes from today's `check_repository_access(authorization: Option, repository_id)`: - **The verified token, both halves of it.** Today the trait takes the raw `Authorization` value, which suits `AuthClientAuthorizer` because it forwards that value upstream to `CheckUserPermission`. An implementation that answers from claims cannot use it without re-parsing and re-verifying a token the interceptor already verified. Neither half alone serves both: `AuthorizationToken` holds claims and no copy of t

entries.title: lore\proposals\2026-08-20-oidc-oauth2-authentication.md
entries.text:
Every non-test caller of `verify_authorization` reads the resource claim directly today, and none
of them goes through `RepositoryAuthorizer`. That breaks Tier 1 outright: its tokens carry no
resource claim, so each of these points denies everything. It also leaves Tier 2 on the
inconsistent readers D4 describes, which disagree on the wildcard. This section therefore moves
every enforcement point onto the same `check_repository_access` call, and the configured
authorizer (D8) decides how it is answered.

A second group needs the same treatment for a different reason.
`check_repository_query_authorization`
([`repository_query.rs`](../../lore-server/src/grpc/handlers/repository_query.rs)) constructs
`AuthClientAuthorizer` directly rather than going through the factory, and the repository-query
handlers call it, so under Tier 1 or Tier 2 they still reach for `CheckUserPermission` on a service
that is not there. They move onto the configured authorizer with the rest. The repository metadata
get and set handlers already take an injected authorizer and only pick up the signature change.

These keep answering denial with `RepositoryNotFound` rather than `permission_denied`. That looks
like an inconsistency and is not one: it stops an unauthorized caller distinguishing a partition
that exists from one that does not, and switching it for uniformity would newly disclose partition
existence by name. The Compatibility note about status codes covers the interceptor path only.

| Call site | Path | Rewired check |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [`auth/jwt_interceptor.rs:71`](../../lore-server/src/auth/jwt_interceptor.rs) | gRPC interceptor | The partition check moves onto the configured authorizer, either inside the interceptor or in the handlers it covers. Synchronous call site. See below. |
| [`repository_query.rs`](../../lore-server/src/grpc/handlers/repository_query.rs) | repository query and get, v0 and v1 | Move onto the configured authorizer, keeping `RepositoryNotFound` on denial. |
| [`quic/storage_service_v4.rs:189`](../../lore-server/src/quic/storage_service_v4.rs) | QUIC storage authorize | Enumerate the caller's grants at session start, once per session, and answer each command's action from them. |
| [`protocol/storage/connect.rs:87`](../../lore-server/src/protocol/storage/connect.rs) | QUIC storage connect | Same, at connect. |
| [`protocol/storage/copy.rs:143`](../../lore-server/src/protocol/storage/copy.rs) | QUIC cross-partition copy, source side | `check_repository_access` on the source partition. |
| [`grpc/storage/v1/copy.rs:83`](../../lore-server/src/grpc/storage/v1/copy.rs) | gRPC cross-partition copy, source side | Same. |
| [`auth/jwt_axum_middleware.rs:40`](../../lore-server/src/auth/jwt_axum_middleware.rs) | HTTP repository routes | Already `async`, so the authorizer call is direct. |
| [`grpc/mod.rs:209`](../../lore-server/src/grpc/mod.rs) | `link_read_authorizer`, cross-partition link reads | Synchronous closure. See below. |

Two of these cannot simply await an authorizer.

**`link_read_authorizer` returns a synchronous closure.** `CanReadRepository` is
`Arc<dyn Fn(RepositoryId) -> bool + Send + Sync>`
([`lore-revision/src/state.rs`](../../lore-revision/src/state.rs)), called during revision-graph
traversal, potentially many times per request. Whatever answers it has to do so without awaiting
anything. Both tiers can: `GlobalGrantsAuthorizer` and `ResourceGrantsAuthorizer`
read a token the interceptor has already verified, so the answer is in memory and the closure needs
no cache, no preload and no staleness bound.

**The gRPC interceptor is synchronous too.** `JWTInterceptor::call` is tonic's `Interceptor`, and
already reaches for `block_in_place` on the JWKS cache miss. A per-request authorization call has to
land somewhere that can answer it without blocking. Two placements do, and picking between them will
be decided at the time of implementation:

- **Keep the check in the interceptor**, against an authorizer that

entries.title: lore\proposals\2026-08-20-oidc-oauth2-authentication.md
entries.text:
Document `UrcAuthApi` and let operators implement it against their own identity provider.

*Rejected because:* it makes every operator write and maintain a gRPC service that duplicates what
their provider already does, and it leaves Lore unable to use any of the ecosystem, Keycloak,
Auth0, Okta, Entra or Dex, without one such service per provider. Those 13 RPCs also include a user
directory and a permission engine, so that service is not a thin one.

entries.title: lore\proposals\2026-08-20-oidc-oauth2-authentication.md
entries.text:
A small stateless service that speaks standard OAuth 2.0 on the front and `UrcAuthApi` on the
back, translating each request and returning the upstream's token unchanged, so an existing
implementation gets the standard interface without changing.

*Rejected because:* building the translation costs about as much as adding the standard endpoints
to the auth service itself, and it does not remove that work, it only defers it, leaving two
services running where one would do. A relay also needs the upstream to emit the adapter's URL as
`iss`, or the adapter has to re-sign tokens, which breaks the no-signing-key goal. And no
`UrcAuthApi` implementation is known outside the deployment this proposal migrates. The idea stays
available without being shipped: an operator who runs such an implementation, or a provider too
quirky for configuration to bridge, can build their own translator against the endpoint mapping in
D1, or extend the provider instead.

entries.title: lore\proposals\2026-08-20-oidc-oauth2-authentication.md
entries.text:
Issue one access token per user, and authorize everything server-side from group and role claims.

*Rejected because:* it discards the property that a token exfiltrated from a build machine unlocks
only the partitions that machine works on. That property is the reason the two-token split
exists, and CI machines holding broadly-scoped credentials is the case it protects. Tier 1 remains
available for deployments that accept the trade, but it does not become the only option.

entries.title: lore\proposals\2026-08-20-oidc-oauth2-authentication.md
entries.text:
[RFC 6749](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6749) §6 permits a refresh-token request to ask for a narrower scope than the original grant,
which maps neatly onto trading the identity credential for a smaller one.

*Rejected as the primary mechanism because:* scope is a flat space-delimited string of values the
provider must know in advance, and Lore's resources are repository/partition IDs created at runtime. Encoding
them as scopes requires the provider to mint scope values it has never seen. That is the same
dynamic-value problem as Tier 2's resource indicators, but with less specification support, since
[RFC 8707](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8707) at least defines the parameter. Refresh-token narrowing stays available as a configured
strategy for providers where it happens to work.

entries.title: lore\proposals\2026-08-20-oidc-oauth2-authentication.md
entries.text:
Let the provider issue opaque access tokens, and have the server call [RFC 7662](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7662) introspection on
every request.

*Rejected because:* it puts a synchronous call to the provider on the path of every storage,
revision and lock operation, which for Lore's request rates makes the provider a throughput ceiling
and a shared failure domain. P1 therefore requires JWT access tokens outright rather than offering
introspection as a fallback, and D8 leaves the setting out until a deployment asks for it.

entries.title: lore\proposals\2026-09-23-per-line-attribution-audit-api.md
lore\proposals\2026-09-23-per-line-attribution-audit-api.md
entries.text:
The query stores nothing ahead of time and computes each answer from scratch in one backward pass.

The walk starts with every line of the file at the requested revision unattributed. It compares that version with the previous one. The lines the comparison reports as changed belong to the current revision. The unchanged lines carry over to the previous version, and the walk repeats. It stops when no line is left unattributed, when it reaches the revision that added the file, or when the budget runs out.

Two properties of Lore keep the walk cheap:

- **Each file node records its predecessors** (`lore-revision/src/node.rs:1826-1844`), and `lore file history` already follows that chain (`lore-revision/src/file/history.rs:600-648`). The walk follows it too, so after its first step it reads only revisions that changed the file. On a sparse instance, where reading an old version can mean a network fetch, this matters.
- **The differ already computes changed regions with line numbers**, and discards them only when it renders patch text (`lore-revision/src/file/diff.rs:900-935`). The walk runs inside `lore-revision` and uses the regions directly. For the same reason the C API needs no new diff event: `lore_file_diff` returns rendered text (`lore-revision/src/file/diff.rs:117-118`).

The walk stops after 100 steps unless the caller changes the budget. The first step compares the requested revision, which need not have changed the file; every later step compares a revision that did. A file changed twice in a repository of ten thousand revisions costs at most three steps.

entries.title: lore\proposals\2026-09-23-per-line-attribution-audit-api.md
entries.text:
The walk stops rather than guesses. When it cannot read a step, it reports every line still unattributed with the reason as its outcome. Lines it already attributed keep their outcome. It never attributes a line to a revision it did not verify.

| Outcome | Cause |
|---|---|
| `obliterated` | `lore file obliterate` removed an old payload. The address remains, the content does not. |
| `binary-in-history` | An older version holds binary content, which the walk cannot compare line by line. |
| `link-unavailable` | The file is in a linked repository that is unauthorized or, offline, unreachable. |
| `content-unavailable` | The content is not local, and `--offline` or an instance with no remote prevents fetching it. |
| `budget-exhausted` | The revision budget ran out. |

These outcomes describe the file or a configured state, and apply to the older versions the walk reads. An environment error, such as a lost connection or content this build cannot decompress, ends the query, and the completion event carries the error. If the error happens during the walk, the query first reports every line: attributed lines keep their outcome, and the lines the walk did not reach get `unresolved`. If it happens before the walk, for example while resolving the revision or reading the requested version, the query reports no ranges. The caller decides whether to show the ranges, the error, or both.

entries.title: lore\proposals\2026-09-23-per-line-attribution-audit-api.md
entries.text:
| Case | Rule |
|---|---|
| Path absent at the requested revision | `FileNotFound`; no walk runs. A deleted path counts as not found |
| Binary file | Error. Classification reuses `make_diff_content` (`lore-revision/src/file/diff.rs:1221-1227`) |
| Empty file | Zero ranges and a successful completion |
| Last line without a terminator | An ordinary line. Adding a terminator changes it |
| Uncommitted edits on disk | Reported as `uncommitted` with no revision, and excluded from the walk. Line numbers are those on disk, so an editor can align them |
| Revision named explicitly | The query ignores the working tree. The file on disk only describes the synced revision, so naming any revision, even the synced one, is a history query |
| No file on disk at the path | Not an edit. A view filter or a sparse instance may leave the path empty on disk, so the revision's lines attribute normally. An empty file on disk has no lines and yields no ranges |
| Recorded rename | Followed. The predecessor of a recorded move is the file node at its old path |
| Unrecorded move (delete plus add) | Not detected. The adding revision owns the added lines |
| Cherry-pick, revert, restore | Not followed. The cherry-pick revision owns the line; its metadata holds the origin hash |
| Path in a linked repository | Followed (`lore-revision/src/file/diff.rs:1255-1263`). Each range names its own repository |
| Content absent locally | Fetched through the existing read path (`lore-revision/src/file/diff.rs:1289-1296`). For an older version, `--offline` reports `content-unavailable` instead |
| Whitespace-only change | Trailing whitespace is ignored by default (`--no-ignore-space-at-eol` turns this off); reindentation counts as a change unless `--ignore-space-change` is given |
| Repeat query for the same revision | Recomputed. Version 1 caches nothing. A consumer can cache on the arguments it passed when it names an explicit revision |
| Comparison rules change in a later release | An answer can change, and the old rules are not kept. A consumer that caches across releases includes the Lore version in its key |

entries.title: lore\proposals\2026-09-23-per-line-attribution-audit-api.md
entries.text:
One record per line spares consumers from expanding ranges.

*Rejected because:* the record count would equal the line count, not the number of changes. `lore-revision/src/branch.rs` has 3,968 lines and 31 revisions that changed it, so per-line output sends 3,968 records where ranges send at most a few hundred. Expanding ranges is trivial for a consumer.

entries.title: lore\proposals\2026-09-23-per-line-attribution-audit-api.md
entries.text:
Each range carries the people, the timestamp and any keys the caller names, so the consumer needs no second call.

*Rejected because:* the same metadata travels once per range instead of once per revision, and the audit API grows with every key a caller wants. `lore revision info` already reports it.

entries.title: lore\proposals\2026-09-23-per-line-attribution-audit-api.md
entries.text:
Mark the lines the walk could not fetch with a reason, as for content an offline instance lacks.

*Rejected because:* a lost connection describes the environment, not the file, and a reason would hide a failure the caller should see. The query ends with the error on the completion event, and the lines it did not reach get `unresolved`.

entries.title: lore\proposals\2026-10-12-machine-level-lore-server-for-containers.md
entries.text:
The machine server's immutable store is a composite store: a `local` tier on the machine's disk and a durable tier in `remote` mode that reaches the upstream's public endpoint through the ordinary client protocol ([`settings.rs`](../../lore-server/src/settings.rs), [`server.rs`](../../lore-server/src/server.rs)).
- **Writes** go to the upstream first, and to the local tier once the upstream accepts them. A put that fully matches the local tier returns without reaching the upstream ([`composite.rs`](../../lore-revision/src/store/composite.rs)).
- **Reads** try the local tier first. A miss goes to the upstream under the same partition, and concurrent misses for one address share one fetch. A detached task writes the result to the local tier once the upstream answers, and a reader that arrives before that write ends takes the fetched result rather than fetching the address again ([`composite.rs`](../../lore-revision/src/store/composite.rs), [`inflight.rs`](../../lore-revision/src/util/inflight.rs)).
- **Capacity.** Eviction runs only when `max_capacity` is set ([`maintenance.rs`](../../lore-storage/src/maintenance.rs)), so the machine server's configuration sets `max_capacity` and `max_size` on its local tier. Neither has a default; the operator sizes `max_size` for the disk the local tier lives on, and `max_capacity` for the index memory the server can spare, since it keeps the whole index loaded (see *Memory*). Every entry is evictable, because the server builds its local store without protection for content not yet durable ([`server.rs`](../../lore-server/src/server.rs)).
- **Isolation.** The server's store isolates partitions ([`server.rs`](../../lore-server/src/server.rs)): it serves a read only from an entry that matches the requested partition, hash and context, and a query reports no other partition's copy ([`immutable_store.rs`](../../lore-storage/src/immutable_store.rs)). A put must carry its payload, which the server hashes against the address ([`put.rs`](../../lore-server/src/protocol/storage/put.rs)), and a copy from another partition checks the session's access to the source ([`storage_service_v4.rs`](../../lore-server/src/quic/storage_service_v4.rs)).
- **Upstream sessions.** Each socket request reaches the upstream under the correlation id its session started with ([`get.rs`](../../lore-server/src/protocol/storage/get.rs)). A session holds its correlation id in the remote tiers until it stops or its connection closes, and while any session holds it, each remote tier keeps one upstream session pool per partition for that correlation id: one session on each upstream connection, which every pool shares ([`storage_service_v4.rs`](../../lore-server/src/quic/storage_service_v4.rs), [`remote.rs`](../../lore-revision/src/store/remote.rs), [`session.rs`](../../lore-transport/src/session.rs)). A container command therefore starts its upstream sessions once per partition in each tier, and commands that interleave on one partition keep each other's pools. Requests that no session's correlation id covers, such as those of the machine server's own gRPC endpoint, share each tier's most recent pool per partition.
- **Upstream connections.** The repositories a remote tier reaches share one set of storage connections to the upstream, `upstream_connections` of them, because the transport caches a connection by remote URL, identity, credential source and authentication mode, not by repository ([`connection.rs`](../../lore-transport/src/connection.rs)). The first use of a repository runs one connect, which every caller waiting on that repository shares, and the tier retries a failed connect with back-off ([`protocol.rs`](../../lore-revision/src/protocol.rs)). The remote tiers size their QUIC windows for 1 Gbit/s at a 100 ms round trip ([`storage_service/client.rs`](../../lore-transport/src/quic/storage_service/client.rs), [`client.rs`](../../lore-transport/src/quic/client.rs)). No setting sizes them from the upstream link yet, as the

entries.title: lore\proposals\2026-10-12-machine-level-lore-server-for-containers.md
entries.text:
The remote tiers are the only paths that reach the upstream as the machine server: forwarded requests carry the caller's token.
- **Configuration.** A remote tier given no identity resolves one from the token store of the user the server runs as: the first identity stored there that the upstream accepts ([`connection.rs`](../../lore-transport/src/connection.rs)). The remote immutable store receives its `auth_url` setting as its identity, and the remote mutable store receives none ([`server.rs`](../../lore-server/src/server.rs), [`settings.rs`](../../lore-server/src/settings.rs)). So the token store of the machine server's user holds the machine identity's login alone. A setting that names the mutable store's identity is follow-up work.
- **Credential.** The identity is a machine identity at the upstream's provider, obtained with the client credentials grant where the provider supports it ([OIDC proposal, D3](2026-08-20-oidc-oauth2-authentication.md#d3-standard-grants-replace-the-custom-rpcs)) or a login stored for the server's user otherwise, readable only by that user. Each machine has its own identity.
- **Scope.** The remote tiers start their sessions per partition, each presenting a token scoped to that partition, for which they exchange the identity ([`remote.rs`](../../lore-revision/src/store/remote.rs), [`sessions.rs`](../../lore-transport/src/quic/storage_service/sessions.rs)). The identity's grants are the union of the repositories the machine's containers use, including repositories they create through the forwarded repository service.
- **Exposure.** A stolen copy of the credential reaches every repository in that union. That is the exposure the OIDC proposal keeps partition-scoped tokens to bound on build machines ([OIDC proposal, Tier 1 only](2026-08-20-oidc-oauth2-authentication.md#tier-1-only-drop-partition-scoped-tokens-entirely)); here it covers one machine's repositories, through a credential that only the machine server's user can read and that the provider rotates and revokes.

entries.title: lore\proposals\2026-10-12-machine-level-lore-server-for-containers.md
entries.text:
Containers would reach the machine server over the machine's network, with today's transports and URL schemes and a host name under the deployment's domain.

*Rejected because:* QUIC always runs TLS ([`server.rs`](../../lore-server/src/server.rs)), so both ends encrypt and decrypt every byte on the same machine, through userspace UDP, at the throughput Goal 5 sets; and every container needs a network route to the host and a certificate it trusts. The benchmark measures QUIC over loopback as a baseline.

entries.title: lore\proposals\2026-10-12-machine-level-lore-server-for-containers.md
entries.text:
A store server would hold one shared store and serve the store traits over a local socket, and the administrator would register each container's repositories.

*Rejected because:* registration cannot confine content. A put without a payload links the payload any partition holds for the hash ([`local/immutable_store.rs`](../../lore-storage/src/local/immutable_store.rs)), so a container that knows a hash reads the content. The machine server inherits the rules that make partition grants hold: a put carries its payload ([`put.rs`](../../lore-server/src/protocol/storage/put.rs)) and a copy checks its source ([`copy.rs`](../../lore-server/src/protocol/storage/copy.rs)).

entries.title: lore\proposals\2026-10-12-machine-level-lore-server-for-containers.md
entries.text:
One Lore service for the whole machine would hold the store and run every container's commands.

*Rejected because:* it would run each container's commands as tasks in one host process, against the host filesystem and outside the container's resource limits, with every path translated between container and host ([`connection.rs`](../../lore/src/remote/connection.rs), [`call.rs`](../../lore/src/remote/call.rs)).

entries.title: lore\proposals\2026-10-12-machine-level-lore-server-for-containers.md
entries.text: *Rejected because:* gRPC carries each fragment as a protobuf message with its payload in a `bytes` field ([`storage.proto`](../../lore-proto/proto/lore/storage/v1/storage.proto)), in HTTP/2 frames of 16 KiB, with receive windows of 2 MiB per stream on the client for reads and 1 MiB on the server for writes by default, which Lore does not change ([hyper `h2/client.rs`](https://github.com/hyperium/hyper/blob/v1.9.0/src/proto/h2/client.rs), [hyper `h2/server.rs`](https://github.com/hyperium/hyper/blob/v1.9.0/src/proto/h2/server.rs)). The storage protocol carries a 12-byte header and the raw payload ([`command_header.rs`](../../lore-transport/src/quic/command_header.rs)).

entries.title: lore\proposals\2026-10-12-machine-level-lore-server-for-containers.md
entries.text:
The machine server would serve the environment itself, check partition access before forwarding, and intercept obliterates to drop its cached copy first.

*Rejected because:* the upstream authorizes each forwarded request for the caller's token, so a second check costs an authorization call per request when `auth_url` is set ([`repository_authorizer.rs`](../../lore-server/src/authnz/repository_authorizer.rs)) without narrowing what a caller reaches; and forwarding by host carries the authentication and notification services with no code per service ([`proxy.rs`](../../lore-server/src/uds/proxy.rs)). Its one gain, dropping an obliterated address from the cache, needs no router: follow-up work has the forwarder decode the admin service's `Obliterate` request alone and drop the address once the upstream accepts it.

entries.title: lore\proposals\2026-10-12-machine-level-lore-server-for-containers.md
entries.text:
Every container would mount one directory holding a storage socket and a gRPC socket.

*Rejected because:* a socket per container lets the server bound each container's connections and buffered bytes (`max_connections_per_socket`, `socket_bytes`), and a container that mounts only its own directory cannot reach another container's socket.

entries.title: lore\proposals\2026-10-12-machine-level-lore-server-for-containers.md
entries.text:
The machine server would reach each forwarded host over one HTTP/2 connection that every container's requests share.

*Rejected because:* a container that stops reading a response fills the shared connection's flow-control window, which stalls every container's forwarded requests to that host until the stream ends. A connection per container and host confines the stall to the container that caused it, at the cost of one upstream connection per container and host, still no more than direct clients open, which hold one per process.

entries.title: lore\proposals\2026-10-12-machine-level-lore-server-for-containers.md
entries.text:
Each process would open several connections, as the QUIC client spreads its requests over streams.

*Rejected because:* each extra connection would cost its own session starts and credit window, which is why every storage client of a process shares one ([`uds/mod.rs`](../../lore-transport/src/uds/mod.rs), [`connection.rs`](../../lore-transport/src/connection.rs)), and requests on one connection already complete out of order. The benchmark decides whether a process needs more.

entries.title: lore\proposals\2026-10-12-machine-level-lore-server-for-containers.md
entries.text: *Rejected because:* no message body exceeds 262,480 bytes: a 256 KiB fragment payload, its command overhead, and 256 bytes for the key `PutResolved` adds ([`uds/mod.rs`](../../lore-transport/src/uds/mod.rs), [`storage_service/mod.rs`](../../lore-transport/src/quic/storage_service/mod.rs), [`types/mod.rs`](../../lore-base/src/types/mod.rs)). Interleaving would therefore save at most the time to send one message, about 2.1 Mbit, or 0.2 ms at 10 Gbit/s, and would cost a reassembly copy on both sides.

entries.title: lore\proposals\2026-10-12-machine-level-lore-server-for-containers.md
entries.text:
A command on the machine would sign tokens for each container with a local key, and the machine server would verify them against a local key set.

*Rejected because:* it adds an issuer, a key to protect and a token format, where containers can carry the tokens Lore already issues and the upstream already accepts, which also lets forwarded requests carry the caller's identity.

entries.title: lore\proposals\2026-10-12-machine-level-lore-server-for-containers.md
entries.text:
The machine server would authorize by which socket a request arrives on, or by the connecting peer's credentials, in place of a token.

*Rejected because:* the authorizer decides from a token and a partition ([`repository_authorizer.rs`](../../lore-server/src/authnz/repository_authorizer.rs)), so it would need a new identity path through every service, and the upstream could not authorize forwarded requests for the caller.

entries.title: lore\proposals\2026-10-12-machine-level-lore-server-for-containers.md
entries.text:
The machine server would forward requests through the forwarding the server has today.

*Rejected because:* it covers six requests and not push ([`forwarded_requests.rs`](../../lore-server/src/grpc/forwarded_requests.rs)), and it targets the upstream's internal endpoint, whose forwarded branch handlers act on the forwarded user id without a check of their own ([`branch_create.rs`](../../lore-server/src/grpc/forwarded_revision/v1/branch_create.rs)).

entries.title: lore\proposals\2026-10-19-instance-move-and-delete.md
entries.text:
Both commands run through `repository_call_no_store` in [`call.rs`](../../lore/src/call.rs). That access mode takes no
`FSLock` and opens only in-memory stores, so after the command reads the instance's `config`, `id` and `instance` files,
this process holds nothing open under the instance directory. This is what lets the rename and the delete succeed on
Windows. A command that needs the real stores opens them itself, for a single step, and closes them before the next
step.

entries.title: lore\proposals\2026-10-19-instance-move-and-delete.md
entries.text:
The commands do not keep other readers out (see [Non-Goals](#non-goals)), so a rename or delete can find the instance's
files in use: another Lore command reading the instance, in the same process or another, or a program the user has open
in it. A finished command in the service process can also keep the instance's stores open for its keep-alive window,
ten seconds by default. Rather than fail at once, each command reissues the file step that was refused, with
exponential backoff, until the reader lets go or a fixed number of attempts is spent:

- **The steps retried.** The rename of a regular instance's directory, by move or by delete's rename aside, and the
  removal of the instance directory or of an SWFS instance's external directory. A removal that is reissued continues
  from what the previous attempt left. Once the rename aside has landed, a reissued removal deletes the sibling alone
  and never renames the path again, since the path may hold a new directory by then. The SWFS remount is not a file
  operation and is not retried. The registration steps already wait for the per-path write token, and are not retried
  either.
- **The errors retried.** Only errors that say the files are in use, so that the step can succeed once they are
  released: a busy resource on every platform, and on Windows access denied, a sharing violation or a lock violation.
  On Unix, `EBUSY` from delete's rename aside marks a mount point, which is deleted in place (see [Delete](#delete)). A
  delete also retries a directory left non-empty, which a reader creating a file during the removal leaves, as does a
  file on Windows whose deletion waits for a handle that is still open. A rename is retried only while its target is
  still free, because Windows reports a rename onto a taken path as access denied, the same error an open file gives.
  Every other error is reported at once.
- **The schedule.** Constants in [`instance.rs`](../../lore-revision/src/instance.rs) set it: the first wait is 50
  milliseconds, each wait doubles up to 2 seconds, and the step is reported as failed after 12 waits, about fifteen
  seconds in all, with the jitter the shared backoff adds. That is longer than the default store keep-alive, so a
  command that has just finished in the same process does not fail a move or delete. The schedule is not configurable.

A step that is still refused when the attempts are spent fails with the same error and instruction as before.

entries.title: lore\proposals\2026-10-19-instance-move-and-delete.md
entries.text:
Keep the status quo: tell users to move the directory and run `update-path`, or to delete it and run `instance prune`.

*Rejected because:* it cannot work for SWFS instances, which have no directory to move or delete. It also gives no
validation before the change and leaves a deleted instance in `instance list` until someone prunes.

entries.title: lore\proposals\2026-10-19-instance-move-and-delete.md
entries.text:
Run the commands as ordinary write commands, then release the repository and run a deferred step. A write-call variant
would take the lock, run the command, flush and drop the repository, and then run the step the command returned.

*Rejected because:* it adds a new variant to the call framework, a way to wait for every store and lock to close, and a
pending-operation type for each command. `NoStore` access gives the same result with no framework change.

entries.title: lore\proposals\2026-10-19-instance-move-and-delete.md
entries.text:
Rename the directory first, then open it at the renamed path to remove its registration, which would close the gap
for a regular instance.

*Rejected because:* it changes the files before the registration step. A deregistration that fails, such as when the
instance cannot be opened, would have to rename the directory back, and a rename back that fails leaves the instance
registered at a path that holds nothing, the state this proposal orders its steps to avoid.

entries.title: lore\proposals\2026-10-19-instance-move-and-delete.md
entries.text:
The behaviour before the amendment that creates the target's parents: the move refused a target whose parent didn't
exist.

*Rejected because:* moving an instance into a new directory took a `mkdir` first, for a step the command can take and
undo itself. The command creates the directories only once every check has passed, so a refused move or a dry run
creates nothing.

entries.title: lore\proposals\2026-10-23-low-level-revision-graph-api.md
entries.text:
Every entry point lives in the `lore_revision_graph_*` namespace, named for the revision graph it operates on. The revision tree proposal already uses the name for the repository-level RPCs: "the existing revision-graph and storage RPCs" ([Non-Goals](2026-05-14-low-level-revision-api.md#non-goals)).

| Surface | Acts on | Identity | Namespace |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Storage system API** | Buffers | `(partition, address)` | `lore_storage_*` |
| **Low-level revision tree API** | One revision's tree | `lore_revision_tree_t` handle | `lore_revision_tree_*` |
| **Low-level revision graph API** | A repository's branches and revisions | `(store, repository)` | `lore_revision_graph_*` |
| **File-system-based revision control API** | A repository instance and its working tree | `globals.repository_path` | `lore_branch_*`, `lore_revision_*`, and others |

Verb names follow the noun-based pattern of `lore-capi`, `lore_revision_graph_<noun>_<verb>`, each with sync and `_async` variants. The Rust entry points live in a new `lore::revision_graph` module, beside `lore::revision_tree`.

entries.title: lore\proposals\2026-10-23-low-level-revision-graph-api.md
entries.text:
There's no handle. Every verb's arguments carry the storage handle (`lore_store_t`) and the repository id (`lore_repository_id_t`, the revision tree proposal's alias for `lore_partition_t`). Each call builds a path-less `RepositoryContext` from those two values for each location it consults (see "Locations"), the way `lore_revision_tree_load` builds its context (`lore/src/revision_tree/handle.rs:325-347`), and drops them when the call returns. Each context has no paths and a zero instance id, and uses the storage handle's local stores. A context that writes carries an in-memory write token. A read verb's contexts carry none, so a write a core makes as a side effect fails instead of reaching the store.

Nothing has to persist between calls. Lore caches the remote connection for each [partition](../glossary.md#partition) (`lore-revision/src/protocol.rs:155-185`), and the storage handle keeps its remote endpoint and the storage session pools it opens (`lore/src/storage/remote.rs:22-77`). A pool serves one `globals.correlation_id` (`lore-transport/src/session.rs:545-547`), so a caller that passes the same correlation id on every call reuses one storage session per connection, as with the storage verbs. The verbs keep their sessions in those pools rather than on the shared connection, so the sessions end with the storage handle.

Every verb enters through the storage handle's in-flight guard, as the storage verbs do (`lore/src/storage/call.rs:68-88`), not through the plain handle lookup the tree load uses (`lore/src/revision_tree/load.rs:129-134`). So `lore_storage_close` behaves as it does for the storage API: it waits for the calls in flight, then flushes the stores (`lore/src/storage/close.rs:7-10`). A verb has no close of its own, so that drain is what flushes its local writes on a disk-backed store. A long push delays a close until the push finishes.

entries.title: lore\proposals\2026-10-23-low-level-revision-graph-api.md
entries.text:
Every verb on this surface follows these rules, and so does every verb added later.

**Arguments.** Each verb's arguments start with these fields:

- `id: u64`, a caller-chosen id echoed back in every event this surface defines for the call
- `store: lore_store_t`
- `repository: lore_repository_id_t`

The storage API documents its per-item `id` the same way (`lore/src/storage/get.rs:67-68`), and the revision tree verbs take the same per-call `id` (`lore/src/revision_tree/commit.rs:56-57`). A verb that takes a batch gives each item its own `id`, as the storage API does. The `id` is separate from `globals.correlation_id`, the string every API uses to key its remote sessions (`lore-transport/src/session.rs:500-546`). `COMPLETE` carries no `id`, as for every C API call, and the callback config that receives it identifies the call.

**Globals.** Every verb ignores `globals.force` and `globals.dry_run`. `branch_sync` and `branch_push` take `force` as an option instead, and no verb has a dry run.

**Locations.** The storage API's per-call flags (`globals.local`, `globals.remote`, `globals.offline`) and the flags the caller opened the storage handle with decide which locations a call consults. The surface shares the storage verbs' veto and rejection rules (`effective_flags`, `lore/src/storage/store.rs:217-246`). The storage API leaves the no-flag default to each verb, and its verbs differ. This surface picks one default for every verb that reports per location. `branch_create` and `branch_archive` follow `obliterate`, which acts on both locations and reports each (`lore/src/storage/obliterate.rs:5-9`). The read verbs consult both as well, whereas storage reads answer from the local store and fall back to the remote (`lore/src/storage/store.rs:114-126`). A branch's local latest and its remote latest are different facts, and a caller that syncs or pushes needs both. A caller that wants one location's answer sets its flag:

- **Neither flag:** The call consults the remote, if the storage handle has one, and the local store. The remote comes first: a write verb writes there before it writes to the local store, and a read verb emits the remote's records first.
- **`local` or `offline`:** The call consults the local store only.
- **`remote`:** The call consults the remote only. On a storage handle without a remote, the call fails with `NoRemote`. The mutable storage verbs reject that case with `InvalidArguments` (`lore/src/storage/mutable_load.rs:92-96`), and storage reads and the tree commit fall back to the local store without saying so (`lore/src/storage/store.rs:119-121`, `lore-capi/lore.h:13131-13136`). This surface names the missing remote instead, because a caller that asks for the remote's answer needs to learn there's no remote, not get the local store's answer in its place.
- **`local` and `remote` together, or flags that contradict the storage handle's:** The call fails with `InvalidArguments`.
- **`branch_sync` and `branch_push`:** These two verbs work across both locations by design, and their sections say what the flags mean for them.

The verbs that report per location (`revision_resolve`, `branch_resolve`, `branch_list`), and `branch_create` and `branch_archive`, reach each location on its own, and the work at one location never touches the other. A verb reaches the local store through a context with no remote, so it never contacts the remote there. On a store that fetches content on demand ([lazy fetch](../glossary.md#lazy-fetch)), a block the local store doesn't hold, whether never fetched or since evicted, counts as absent for the local answer. A corrupt block or a failed read still fails the call at that location. A read verb writes nothing to the local store, and work at the remote neither writes to the local store nor reads from it. The file-system verbs differ here in two ways:

- They cache a remote branch's name-to-id mapping and metadata, and the repository metadata, in the local store (`lore-revision/src/branch.rs

entries.title: lore\proposals\2026-10-23-low-level-revision-graph-api.md
entries.text:
The verbs reuse Lore's branch model, RPCs, and cores, but the cores assume the file-system verbs' behavior in places. Each change below stays inside the Lore library, the transport client, the core Lore Server shares with them, that core's call sites in Lore Server, Lore Server's `BranchPush` and `BranchMetadataSet` handlers, and the local and DynamoDB mutable stores. None changes a Lore Server protocol message or field, or an on-disk structure.

- **Per-location contexts:** The verbs reach the local store through a context with no remote, which the context constructor already allows (`lore-revision/src/repository.rs:661-667, 674-683`). At the remote, they skip the cores' local caching of mutable keys (`lore-revision/src/branch.rs:704-713`, `lore-revision/src/repository.rs:3852`) and the number lookup's write of fetched revision states (`lore-revision/src/revision.rs:1679`, `lore-revision/src/find.rs:317-340`). Their remote context's immutable reads skip the local store (`lore-storage/src/options.rs:107-110`) and suppress local caching, even for blocks flagged for local caching. That takes a new `ReadOptions` field (`lore-storage/src/options.rs:100-131`, `lore-storage/src/read.rs:353-355, 1815-1817`) and a context setting that `read_options_from_repository` passes to the cores' reads (`lore-revision/src/immutable.rs:134-147`). At the remote, they call the RPCs themselves rather than the cores that read the `remote` flag from the globals, such as the resolver's branch lookup (`lore-revision/src/branch.rs:1032-1040`). In the local store, a read verb skips the name lookup's derived-id write (`lore-revision/src/branch.rs:715-721`).
- **Local misses:** Reads in the local store tell a block the store doesn't hold apart from a corrupt entry or a failed read, through another `ReadOptions` field that only the new verbs set, and only for the local store. All three come back as `AddressNotFound` today (`lore-storage/src/read.rs:244-257, 461-462, 518-522`). Every other read keeps today's answer, including Lore Server's, whose `AddressNotFound` drives the push's re-upload recovery (`lore-revision/src/branch/push.rs:1928-1936`).
- **Ancestry walk:** When it has no remote to ask, the shared branch-point walk fails once neither side can advance and one of them is stuck on a revision the local store lacks, reporting that revision, instead of looping (`lore-revision/src/history.rs:167-253`). The file-system push, sync, and revision lookup run the same walk (`lore-revision/src/branch/push.rs:719, 877`, `lore-revision/src/revision/sync.rs:603`, `lore-revision/src/revision.rs:1600`), so a push or sync without a remote now fails instead of looping, and a revision lookup falls back to the local latest, as it already does on any walk error (`lore-revision/src/revision.rs:1611-1616`). Compatibility lists the change.
- **Resolution per location:** The resolver merges both locations into one answer when it searches both (`lore-revision/src/revision.rs:1597-1622, 1656-1705`) and returns only a hash. `revision_resolve` doesn't call it, because the resolver's fallback walk reads and writes the local store (`lore-revision/src/revision.rs:1634-1710`). At the remote, the verb calls `branch_query` and `revision_list` itself. In the local store, it reads the local latest and walks the parent history with a walk that reads only the local store and writes nothing. It then reads the revision record for the rest.
- **Push core:** Gains an option to check linked revisions on the remote instead of pushing them (`lore-revision/src/branch/push.rs:1786-1830`), takes `force` and `dry_run` as parameters instead of reading the globals (`lore-revision/src/branch/push.rs:1012, 1037, 1186-1187`), and returns its outcome, which today reaches the caller only as events (`lore-revision/src/branch/push.rs:613-619, 1299-1310, 1351-1360`). Its history walk and upload become reachable from the `lore` crate (`lore-revision/src/branch/push.rs:785, 922`). For this surface it also update

entries.title: lore\proposals\2026-10-23-low-level-revision-graph-api.md
lore\proposals\2026-10-23-low-level-revision-graph-api.md
entries.text:
This namespace is the home for repository-level verbs that need no repository instance. An amendment to this proposal can add a later verb when it meets all of these conditions:

- It's stateless and takes `(store, repository)`.
- It follows every rule under "Conventions": location flags, separate work at each location, records per location, the revision selector, branch ids, error detail, and event naming.
- It needs no new RPC, Lore Server protocol message, or on-disk structure. Its command and events join the Lore service IPC by appending, as this proposal's do.
- It doesn't change Lore Server's behavior.
- It doesn't change the trust model.

An amendment adds a subsection to "Extensions" below, giving the verb, its arguments, its events, and its error codes, and updates `updated` in the frontmatter. Its author proposes it as a [change request](../glossary.md#change-request) or pull request against this file. Reviewers discuss and accept it under the LEP process in `GOVERNANCE.md`, like the proposal itself, before anyone implements the verb. The subsection stays marked Draft until then. If reviewers reject the amendment, its subsection stays in the file, marked Rejected, as rejected proposals stay in the tree. A verb that breaks a condition above, such as one that needs a protocol or format change, changes Lore Server's behavior, or introduces a stateful handle, needs a new proposal, and so does any change to the conventions themselves.

These verbs are likely candidates, though this proposal proposes none of them:

- Reading a branch record by id
- Reading and editing branch metadata and protection
- Reading repository metadata, such as the default branch
- Restoring an archived branch
- Listing a branch's revisions
- Walking history and finding merge bases
- Diffing two revisions
- A merging sync of a divergent local latest

entries.title: lore\proposals\2026-10-23-low-level-revision-graph-api.md
entries.text:
Add `branch_create` and `push` to `lore_revision_tree_*`, resolve a branch's latest with a load verb that takes a branch, and list branches from a handle loaded at the zero revision.

*Rejected because:* listing and resolving act on the repository, not on a tree. List would need a tree loaded only to stand in for its repository, and resolve would load a tree only to read its hash. The repository-level verbs the revision tree proposal deferred would need a home anyway, which would split branch operations across two namespaces.

entries.title: lore\proposals\2026-10-23-low-level-revision-graph-api.md
entries.text:
Give `lore_branch_*` a mode in which a storage handle and a repository id replace `globals.repository_path`.

*Rejected because:* those verbs' meaning depends on the instance:

- List reports `is_current`.
- Create takes its parent from the current branch and switches the instance (`lore-revision/src/branch/create.rs:104-129, 216-221`).
- Push without a branch pushes the current one (`lore-revision/src/branch/push.rs:292, 512`).
- `switch`, the `merge_*` verbs, and `reset` act on a working tree.

An instance-free mode would give each verb its own exceptions and make the same verb behave differently depending on how the caller reached it.

entries.title: lore\proposals\2026-10-23-low-level-revision-graph-api.md
entries.text:
`lore_revision_graph_open(store, repository)` returns a handle that every verb takes, with a matching `lore_revision_graph_close`.

*Rejected because:* a handle would hold nothing Lore doesn't already cache per partition, and it would bring a lifecycle to specify: close ordering against the storage handle, teardown when an IPC connection drops, and draining in-flight calls. Stateless verbs avoid all of it, and a later proposal can still add a handle-taking verb if one needs state across calls.

entries.title: lore\proposals\2026-10-23-low-level-revision-graph-api.md
entries.text:
Give every verb an optional instance id. Local operations would then act as that instance does: a branch's local current would be that instance's current revision, and a local sync would move that instance's current anchor.

*Rejected because:*

- For reads, the instance records already report every instance on a branch with its current revision, so an instance id would only filter what the caller can filter itself.
- For writes, an instance's current and staged anchors describe its working tree. Moving them from outside the instance leaves the working tree not matching the anchor, and races the instance's own commands. Those commands take the repository lock, and a storage handle never does ([ADR-00024](../developing/decisions/00024-store-locks-held-per-span-contain-the-repository-lock.md)). Avoiding both means taking the instance's locks, respecting its staged state, and updating its working tree, which is the file-system API's job.
- Every verb would have two meanings depending on whether a caller passed an instance, the same objection the alternative of running the file-system verbs without an instance meets.

A virtual instance whose working tree derives from its current anchor, such as a clone served through a virtual file system, is the one case where moving an instance's current from outside would be a real sync. It needs its own contract with the instance's locks and staged state, and so a proposal of its own.

entries.title: lore\proposals\2026-10-23-low-level-revision-graph-api.md
entries.text:
Document the branch key derivation, and let callers read and write branch state through `lore_storage_mutable_*`.

*Rejected because:*

- It would make an internal key layout a public contract, the same lock-in the revision tree proposal rejected for the node block format ([Expose the internal node block format directly](2026-05-14-low-level-revision-api.md#expose-the-internal-node-block-format-directly)).
- It still couldn't publish, because Lore Server refuses generic writes to branch latest pointers and metadata (`lore-server/src/protocol/storage/mutable_store_handler.rs:52-72`).
- It can't list remote branches, because `mutable_list` is local-only.

entries.title: lore\proposals\2026-10-23-low-level-revision-graph-api.md
entries.text:
Swap a branch's metadata and its name's mapping in one conditional write, as DynamoDB's `TransactWriteItems` allows (`lore-aws/src/dynamodb.rs:539`), so a restore needs no `restoring` and `released` keys.

*Rejected because:* the `MutableStore` contract swaps one key at a time, and every store, plugin and remote store would need a swap over two. The local store would take two buckets under one lock, and a remote mutable store reaches Lore Server through the storage protocol's single-key swap, so a two-key swap would need a new protocol message, which the Non-Goals rule out.

entries.title: lore\proposals\2026-10-23-low-level-revision-graph-api.md
entries.text:
Let `lore branch switch` and `lore branch reset` onto an archived branch, given its id, restore it, claiming the name and recording the restore as a create does.

*Rejected because:* a create given the id already restores the branch, and `lore push` makes one on its own. A switch or reset that restores would repeat the create's record, claim and settle in two more places, and one that mapped the name while a create restored the branch under another name would leave it mapped from both.

entries.title: lore\proposals\2026-10-23-low-level-revision-graph-api.md
entries.text:
Accept `main@latest`, `main@25`, `main@<hash>`, and `~N`, as the CLI does.

*Rejected because:*

- An identifier without a branch means the branch the instance is on (`lore-revision/src/revision.rs:1765`), and there's no instance.
- A parsed string makes every caller round-trip through text.
- A structured selector says exactly what it names, and turning a string into one is the caller's choice.

entries.title: lore\proposals\2026-10-29-swfs-through-the-filesystem-provider.md
entries.text:
The interface has two traits (`lore-revision/src/fs/filesystem_provider.rs`):

- **`FilesystemProvider`** creates operations. `begin_operation` returns an `Arc<InstanceOperationImpl>`. For `OsFilesystem` this is a stateless wrapper around the working-tree root. For `SwfsFilesystem` it is where the provider freezes the mount. One provider covers a whole mounted filesystem, so links and layers below it share the operation their parent holds.
- **`InstanceOperation`** performs reads and writes against the operation's view of the working tree.

`with_operation(filesystem, work)` and `with_operation_if(filesystem, needed, work)` are the only ways commands open an operation. They call `finalize` whether or not `work` succeeds, so a failure never leaves a mount frozen. They report the work's own error ahead of a finalize error (G3). `with_operation_if` lets a command that reads the tree only under some conditions skip the freeze entirely.

`InstanceOperationImpl` wraps a `StaticDispatchInstanceOperation` enum (`Os`, `Swfs`, and `Test` under the `test-util` feature). It forwards each trait method through a `match`. `InstanceOperation`'s async methods return `impl Future` and are not boxed, so the OS path compiles to direct calls (G6). Concerns that every provider shares live in the wrapper and not in each provider:

- **Dry run.** Every write method returns early when the execution context is a dry run. No provider has to implement dry-run handling itself.
- **Change tracking.** Each write records that it happened (`record_change`), and `finalize` passes `changes_made` to the provider. SWFS uses this to decide whether the thaw invalidates anything.
- **Recorded modification times and the clock floor.** These are collected per operation (`record_modified_time`, `clock_floor`), so the caller that knows which revision the operation leaves current commits them.

`RepositoryContext::file_system()` (`lore-revision/src/repository.rs`) returns the instance's provider. It defaults to `OsFilesystem` for the working-tree path. It is `InvalidFilesystemProvider` (`lore-revision/src/fs/invalid_filesystem_provider.rs`) for contexts that must never touch a working tree, such as the store-holder contexts and the context a mount uses internally. If code reaches the filesystem by mistake from one of these contexts, it gets an error instead of silently reading the wrong directory.

entries.title: lore\proposals\2026-10-29-swfs-through-the-filesystem-provider.md
entries.text:
This phase addresses G4 and G6. It ships before any SWFS behavior and changes nothing a user can observe.

1. **Introduce the traits and `OsFilesystem`/`OsOperation`** (`lore-revision/src/fs/os/mod.rs`). Each `OsOperation` method calls the same `lore-io` driver call the command made before. `RepositoryContext` gains a `file_system` field defaulting to `OsFilesystem::new(path)`, and server contexts get an empty-path provider. Nothing calls the new code yet.
2. **Move call sites one command at a time.** Each change wraps a command's working-tree access in `with_operation(repository.file_system(), …)` and replaces direct I/O with operation methods: `file/info.rs`, `file/hash.rs`, `file/dirty.rs`, `file/stage.rs`, `file/unstage.rs`, `file/reset.rs`, `file/write.rs`, `file/obliterate.rs`, `file/diff.rs`, `diff.rs`, `commit.rs`, `branch/merge.rs`, `revision/sync.rs` and `fs/realize.rs`. With only `OsOperation` behind the seam, each change is a refactor. The existing unit and smoke tests are the oracle, and a regression can be traced to one reviewable, revertible change.
3. **Lift the shared concerns into `InstanceOperationImpl`** (dry run, change tracking, modified times) as separate changes, each removing the duplicate handling from the command it replaces.
4. **Add a test provider** (`StaticDispatchInstanceOperation::Test`, `filesystem_provider::test_util`). Tests use it to assert operation boundaries: each command finalizes exactly once, reports `changes_made` correctly, and finalizes after a failure. See `lore-revision/tests/unit/fs/filesystem_provider.rs`.

Once phase 0 is done, every working-tree access is routed through one point that a second provider can occupy.

entries.title: lore\proposals\2026-10-29-swfs-through-the-filesystem-provider.md
entries.text:
- **Configuration.** `RepositoryConfig.vfs: Option<VfsConfig>` with `VfsType::{None, Swfs}` (`lore-revision/src/repository.rs`). `RepositoryConfig::validate` refuses SWFS without a shared store, because the mount serves reads from the immutable store. This is also what lets several SWFS instances of one repository share one copy of each file's content: every mount reads from the same store, and only an instance's write directory holds anything of its own.
- **Where an instance lives.** An SWFS instance's `.lore` and its SWFS `write` directory live in the external instance directory (`external_dir_for_instance`), not inside the mount.
- **Mount lifecycle.** `MountManagerState` (`lore-revision/src/fs/mount_manager_state.rs`) holds one `MountManager` per service process. The service initializes it on startup (`lore/src/service/initialization.rs`) and remounts every SWFS instance it finds in the shared-store registry (`MountManager::mounts_of_entries`). Opening an SWFS instance outside the service is an error (`repository.rs`, "Loading a SWFS repository without using the service").
- **Serving reads.** `MountResources` (`lore-revision/src/fs/swfs/mount_resources.rs`) holds the mount's own `RepositoryContext` and the `State` it presents. `read_file` resolves the path to a node and reads the requested range from the immutable store. `enumerate_directory` lists a node's children with their sizes and recorded modification times.
- **What the user changed.** `ModifiedTree` (`modified_tree.rs`) holds the files SWFS reports as changed as an in-memory `State` that carries only `Dirty*` flags, apart from the staged `State`. The `notify_*` callbacks feed it, and it rebuilds from `swfsGetModifiedFileList` where it may have missed a change. A move is a deletion of the origin and an addition of the destination. SWFS lists the origin as a deletion carrying the destination's `file_index`, and Lore pairs the two ([ADR-00029](../developing/decisions/00029-swfs-modified-file-record.md)).
- **A rule for every stage.** Lore does not walk an SWFS instance's tree through the OS filesystem. A walk lists every directory and reads what it finds, which fills SWFS's cache with the tree the mount exists to leave unfetched. Reads come from the served tree, the immutable store, the frozen snapshot (`FrozenSnapshot`, `swfsReadFrozenFile`) and the operation's own writes. The mount is read through the OS only where nothing else holds the answer, such as a record that failed to rebuild, and a path the operation wrote itself.
- **Never write the revision's own changes through the OS.** In the SWFS code paths, Lore does not write, rename or remove a file or directory of the repository through the mount path to apply a change to what a revision serves. A write through the mount is indistinguishable from the user's own change: SWFS records it as modified and reports it as one, so Lore's changes and the user's become one set. Freeze and thaw are atomic only if the changes that arrive through the mount are the user's while Lore describes its own to the thaw. Mixing them breaks what Lore needs from that atomicity: that a thaw commits exactly what Lore names, that what SWFS reports modified is the user's work, and that a user's uncommitted change is never replaced by a description of the source. What a revision holds, and what a sync, clone, branch switch or commit changes in it, such as a write, a move, a case change or a removal, is described to the thaw. Two kinds of write go through the mount. Scratch files, such as the `~base`, `~mine` and `~theirs` copies a merge leaves for the user, are not part of any revision. And an edit Lore makes on the user's behalf, whose result differs from the current revision, is a user edit: a merge or resolve result, a cherry-pick or `revert --no-commit` result, and the content a dependency sync keeps from an older revision. SWFS holds these as the user's changes, which they are, and they are read, staged and committed as such. What the

entries.title: lore\proposals\2026-10-29-swfs-through-the-filesystem-provider.md
entries.text:
Goal: serve a revision through SWFS. Freeze/thaw has to work only in its simplest form: the mount starts empty, so nothing the user wrote needs reconciling.

- `create_local` and the clone path call `MountManager::create_mount`, which mounts an empty view of the instance, and then `get_mount_filesystem_provider`, which builds the `SwfsFilesystem` that the new `RepositoryContext` holds.
- Clone runs its ordinary realize path through the operation. `SwfsOperation::write_node` and `set_file_to_immutable_store_contents` make sure the content is in the local store (`immutable::read`) and record the path as touched. They write no bytes to the mount. `create_dir_all`, `write_file`, `make_executable` and `remove_recursive` only record the path.
- `finalize` thaws (`SwfsInterface::thaw`). It reloads the presented `State` from the current anchor (`MountResources::update_state`). It describes every touched path and its ancestors, sorted parent-first, to `swfsThaw`, which SWFS requires (`swfs/state.rs::written_files`). At this stage the thaw only publishes the tree, because the mount held nothing a user could have changed.
- `SwfsOperation::file_info` answers from the presented `State`. `update_state` reloads that `State` only inside `thaw`, so within an operation it still holds the tree from before the operation began. In stage 1 the mount starts empty, so every path the clone writes reads back as absent until the thaw. Clone tolerates this. `set_file_to_immutable_store_contents` reports no file information, so `set_file_to_node` (`repository/clone.rs`) falls back to `file_info` and finds no file. It therefore records a modification time of zero and leaves the executable bit alone, since an absent file reports no bit to compare against. The sync realize path reads nothing back: it takes the `FileInfo` that `write_node` builds from the node (`fs/realize.rs`). Stage 5's modification-time edge case covers making read-backs see what the operation has written.
- The working-tree diff and content reads (`changes_from_filesystem_to_state`, `read_directory`, `content_source`, `file_holds_content`) stay delegated to `OsOperation` (`fake_with_os!` in `swfs/filesystem.rs`). Stage 1 does not claim that `status`, `stage` or `commit` are correct on an SWFS instance.
- Clone refuses `--dry-run` with `--vfs swfs`, because a mount cannot be taken back (`repository/clone.rs`).

What users get: `lore repository clone --vfs swfs` and `lore repository create --vfs swfs` produce a browsable working tree whose files load on first read.

entries.title: lore\proposals\2026-10-29-swfs-through-the-filesystem-provider.md
entries.text:
Goal: move a mounted instance from one revision to another by updating what SWFS presents, without materializing files and without overwriting the user's local changes.

- `sync` runs the ordinary realize path (`fs/realize.rs`) through the operation, with the same local-change checks, options and per-file events as on disk. Nothing in `sync` is specific to SWFS.
- Each write the realize path makes records an intent instead of writing bytes ([ADR-00031](../developing/decisions/00031-swfs-realize-operation-results-the-revision-does-not-hold.md)). At finalize, the provider realizes the results the revision does not hold, such as merge sidecars, to the mount ([ADR-00030](../developing/decisions/00030-swfs-merge-writes-go-to-the-filesystem.md)). It then loads the served tree for the new revision and describes each path the operation touched to `swfsThaw`, as that tree serves it: a file with its size and times, a directory as a directory, and a path the tree no longer serves as holding nothing.
- A path the operation left alone, where the old and new revisions differ and SWFS holds no change, keeps what the working tree held: a path the old revision served has that content written to the mount, and a path only the new revision has is recorded as absent and not served (`keep_unwritten_changes`, [ADR-00032](../developing/decisions/00032-swfs-serve-views-and-partial-trees.md)). This is what a disk sync does when it leaves a file alone.
- To know which paths carry local changes, the provider reads the modified-file record (`ModifiedTree`), which SWFS's own list backs. It needs the paths, and the list does not carry content.
- A path that changes between file and directory in one sync, or only in the case of its name, is described as its end state in a single thaw. SWFS replaces the node and takes the spelling the description gives it (`swfs.h`, `swfsThaw`). Lore adds no step of its own for either.
- Dependency-set syncs, resets of local changes and syncs that carry layers need nothing more than the ordinary path, so `sync` refuses none of them on SWFS.

What users get: `lore sync` on an SWFS instance, with the same local-change refusals and options as on disk.

entries.title: lore\proposals\2026-10-29-swfs-through-the-filesystem-provider.md
entries.text:
Goal: read the user's writes out of a frozen mount and commit them through the ordinary commit path.

- `changes_from_filesystem_to_state` answers from the modified-file record instead of walking (`record_diff.rs`). This is the optimization G2 exists for: `status`, `stage` and `commit` visit only what the user touched, and never hydrate an unmodified file. A record that may have missed a change is untrusted until rebuilt from SWFS's list.
- `content_source` and `file_holds_content` answer through a view of the operation (`SwfsView`, `view.rs`). A file SWFS holds changed is read from its frozen snapshot (`swfsReadFrozenFile`), a file the operation wrote comes from the operation's own writes, and anything else comes from the served tree and the immutable store, so an unmodified file is never read through the mount.
- Commit names each file it stores and each node it deletes (`InstanceOperationImpl::committed_path`). The thaw that ends the commit describes them as the committed revision serves them, so SWFS drops its record that the user changed them. Without this, SWFS keeps the change, and a later thaw naming a path SWFS still holds as deleted is taken as the commit of that deletion, not as new content.
