- A write the user makes during a freeze is not Lore's to describe. The thaw leaves it alone, so it behaves as if the user wrote it after the thaw, and it appears in the next modified-file list. Where what Lore expects conflicts with such a write, for example a different spelling, the user's version wins, and `reset` returns to Lore's.
- `commit` of a link alone or of a layer needs no refusal, because the provider needs no revision handed to it: the next thaw loads the served tree from what the instance has stored.

What users get: `status`, `stage`, `commit` and `reset` on an SWFS instance, with the same semantics as on disk.

entries.title: lore\proposals\2026-10-29-swfs-through-the-filesystem-provider.md
entries.text:
Goal: a mounted instance presents, syncs and commits its links and layers as an on-disk instance does.

A link places another repository's tree at a path in the parent (`LinkMountInfo`), and a layer overlays another repository's files at a path (`LayerMountInfo`, `lore-revision/src/state.rs`). Each has its own `RepositoryContext` and `State`. On disk they share the parent's provider and operation: one provider covers the whole mounted filesystem (`FilesystemProvider::begin_operation` docs). Stage 4 keeps that shape. A link or layer stays a subtree of the parent's mount and is never a second mount ([ADR-00034](../developing/decisions/00034-swfs-serve-links-and-layers.md)).

- **Serving.** The served tree resolves a path across the link and layer mount points. A path below a link reads its node from the linked repository's state, at the pin the staged state holds, and its content from that repository's store. A path below a layer reads from the layer's current revision where the layer holds a node there. Their files stay virtual.
- **Sync and mount changes.** The ordinary realize path covers links and layers. When a link or layer is added, repinned or removed, the thaw describes the mount path as the directory it mounts, and names the files below it only where the user changed them, rather than naming every file of a repinned tree. A local change below a link is kept, as on disk. Removing a link or layer, and `reset --purge`, name each file SWFS holds of the user's below the path in the same thaw, which deletes it, because naming a directory leaves what the user holds below it. A directory the user made stays, which no thaw removes.
- **Commit.** A commit of a link alone or of a layer is allowed, with no refusal. The thaw after it loads the served tree from what the instance stored, so the new pin or revision is served.
- **Change detection.** The modified-file record holds paths below a link or layer as it holds any path, so a diff that crosses a mount point is answered from the record. A diff the record does not answer, such as one measured from another revision, walks the operation's own state rather than the mount.

What users get: repositories that use links and layers work on SWFS, with the same sync and commit behavior as on disk.

entries.title: lore\proposals\2026-10-29-swfs-through-the-filesystem-provider.md
lore\proposals\2026-10-29-swfs-through-the-filesystem-provider.md
entries.text:
Mount SWFS at the working-tree path and keep `OsFilesystem`. Lore would write and walk files through the driver like any other directory.

*Rejected because:* every write during clone and sync would pass through the driver into the write directory, which costs the same disk and time as materializing and removes the reason for SWFS. Every status walk would hydrate the files it reads. A plain directory has no freeze/thaw window, so Lore could not update the presented tree atomically against user writes.

entries.title: lore\proposals\2026-10-29-swfs-through-the-filesystem-provider.md
entries.text:
Define the seam as `open`/`read`/`write`/`stat`/`readdir` and have SWFS implement each one.

*Rejected because:* that altitude cannot express "diff this subtree", "write this node" or "does this file hold this content". SWFS would have to emulate a disk file by file, and could never answer from its modified-file list or skip writing bytes. Nor can it express an operation as a freeze window. G2 would be unreachable.

entries.title: lore\proposals\2026-10-29-swfs-through-the-filesystem-provider.md
entries.text:
Branch on `config.is_swfs()` inside `sync`, `commit`, `status` and the rest, and write SWFS versions of each.

*Rejected because:* the rules those commands encode (filters, case folding, modes, dirty/stage flags, local-modification checks, dry runs) would exist twice and drift apart. That is the failure G1 exists to prevent. Under the chosen design, a provider that holds state still shares `hold.rs`, the commit path and the event reporting.

entries.title: lore\proposals\2026-10-29-swfs-through-the-filesystem-provider.md
entries.text:
Make `InstanceOperation` object-safe and box each async method's future.

*Rejected because:* the OS path would pay a heap allocation per file operation on the hottest loops (status walks, realize), which G6 rules out. The provider itself is `dyn` (`Arc<dyn FilesystemProvider>`), because it is called once per command.

entries.title: lore\proposals\2026-10-31-copy-on-write-instance-clone.md
entries.text:
All measured figures come from one machine: an Apple M3 Max (Mac15,9) with 64 GB of memory and its internal
SSD, an APFS volume, macOS 26.6. The tree is the partial view above, with a built C++ editor in it. Lore is a
release build of a prototype of this design.

- Times are wall-clock times from `/usr/bin/time -p`.
- Disk use is the volume's free space from `df` before and after, since `du` counts cloned blocks once for
  each file that shares them.
- The clone range covers the 17 clones of the tree recorded over three days. The scan range covers three
  clones.

Nothing was measured on Windows, on Linux, or on a full ~1 TB tree. Figures for those are estimates, labelled
as such where they appear, with their basis; Unresolved Questions lists the measurements that would confirm
them.

entries.title: lore\proposals\2026-10-31-copy-on-write-instance-clone.md
entries.text:
Lore already reaches an instance's files through its filesystem provider (`FilesystemProvider` in
`lore-revision/src/fs/filesystem_provider.rs`), with an OS provider for on-disk instances and an SWFS provider
for virtual ones. This proposal gives the provider two responsibilities for a clone (Goal 3):

- **Answer what a clone would do, before anything is written.** Given a source instance and a destination,
  the provider answers one of:
  - *shares blocks*: the clone costs metadata, not content;
  - *copies bytes*: the clone writes N bytes in M files, with the free space at the destination;
  - *unsupported*: no clone is possible, with a reason naming the filesystem or provider.
- **Perform the clone** it described, and report what it did: how many entries it cloned and how many it
  copied.

[Sync prefetch](2026-11-04-sync-prefetch.md) reuses this interface and its clone backends to place
individual files from its cache, and adds the questions it needs; this proposal does not depend on it.

A provider that does not implement these answers *unsupported*, so a provider that predates this proposal,
or one that cannot yet clone, makes the clone refuse rather than guess.

#### Clone backends

The OS provider does its part through clone backends, one per filesystem rather than per OS:

- **APFS** (macOS): [`clonefile(2)`](https://keith.github.io/xcode-man-pages/clonefile.2.html), which shares
  every block of a file or directory and fails rather than copies when it cannot.
- **Reflink** (Linux: Btrfs, XFS, bcachefs):
  [`FICLONE`](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/ioctl_ficlone.2.html) per file, which shares the file's
  extents and fails with an error, not a copy, when the filesystem cannot.
- **ReFS and Dev Drive** (Windows):
  [`FSCTL_DUPLICATE_EXTENTS_TO_FILE`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/winioctl/ni-winioctl-fsctl_duplicate_extents_to_file),
  ReFS [block cloning](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/storage/refs/block-cloning), which
  reports whether it cloned. The backend does not rely on
  [`CopyFileEx`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/winbase/nf-winbase-copyfileexw) to clone:
  it block-clones only on Windows 11 24H2 and Windows Server 2025, falls back to a byte copy silently
  elsewhere, and does not say which it did.
- **Copy**: a plain byte copy, for every other filesystem (NTFS, ext4, network shares) and for a destination
  on another volume. It answers *copies bytes*, and an instance clone runs it only with `--allow-copy`.

A backend knows filesystems, not Lore: it clones and copies paths and reports what it did, and holds no
instance IDs, anchors or locks. The provider owns identity, exclusions and locking. Adding a filesystem or an
OS means adding one backend.

**Detection is per pair of directories.** For a source and a destination, the OS provider probes for real:
it writes a small file in the source's Lore directory, clones it into the destination's parent with each
candidate backend, and removes both. Only volumes of two different filesystems get the copy backend without
a probe. Volume identifiers (`st_dev` on Unix, the volume serial number on Windows) decide nothing: Btrfs
gives each subvolume its own `st_dev` although `FICLONE` works between them, and two copies of one virtual
disk can carry the same serial number. The first backend whose probe shares blocks
is the answer; if none does, the answer is *copies bytes*. A probe that fails for another reason, such as no
permission to write in the Lore directory, fails the clone. The probe, not the OS or the filesystem's name,
decides, so a Windows machine with an NTFS system drive and a Dev Drive gets the right answer for each, and a
filesystem mounted without reflink support gets *copies bytes*.

**A promise of sharing holds for the whole clone.** If the backend chosen for *shares blocks* fails to clone
an entry partway through, the clone stops and fails, rather than copying that entry, unless `--allow

entries.title: lore\proposals\2026-10-31-copy-on-write-instance-clone.md
entries.text:
A full copy of a 1 TB tree takes hours and holds the store's locks throughout, so the clone never makes one
unasked (Goal 4).

- **Without `--allow-copy`**, a clone whose answer is *copies bytes* or *unsupported* refuses before writing
  anything. The message names the source's and destination's filesystems and volumes and the remedy: put
  the instances on a filesystem that clones (Dev Drive or ReFS on Windows, APFS on macOS, Btrfs, XFS or
  bcachefs on Linux) and the destination on the same volume as the source. For *copies bytes*, it also says what
  `--allow-copy` would cost.
- **With `--allow-copy`**, the clone states before it starts that it will copy N GB in M files and hold the
  store's locks throughout, so Lore commands wait for it as Lock hold describes. It
  refuses when the destination's free space is below the bytes it would copy.
- When the backend shares blocks, `--allow-copy` only lets the clone copy the entries that turn out not to
  clone. It does nothing for *unsupported*, which always refuses.

entries.title: lore\proposals\2026-10-31-copy-on-write-instance-clone.md
entries.text:
A clone shares blocks with its source only for files neither has rewritten since. Each file a sync or a build
writes into either instance is a private copy, so a clone that syncs forward, or builds, stops sharing those
files, and a clone that tracks a fast-moving branch converges towards a full copy. Deleting the source frees
nothing the clone still shares. Measure a clone's real cost with the volume's free space (`df`); `du` counts
each shared block once per file and overstates it. A clone therefore suits workspaces that diverge little
from their source or live briefly: an agent's task, a bisect, a review, a one-off build.

entries.title: lore\proposals\2026-10-31-copy-on-write-instance-clone.md
entries.text:
An earlier draft of this proposal copied whenever the filesystem could not clone.

*Rejected because:* on NTFS or across volumes that turns a minutes-long command into one that writes up to
1 TB and holds every instance's store locks for hours, without warning. Refusing, with an opt-in that states
the cost, keeps that choice with the user.

entries.title: lore\proposals\2026-10-31-copy-on-write-instance-clone.md
entries.text:
Pick block cloning per target OS at build time and find out per file whether it cloned, as the prototype does.

*Rejected because:* the filesystem decides, not the OS. A Windows machine can hold NTFS and Dev Drive
volumes side by side, Linux has both ext4 and reflink filesystems, and no filesystem clones across volumes.
Knowing only per file, after writing, rules out refusing before the clone starts.

entries.title: lore\proposals\2026-10-31-copy-on-write-instance-clone.md
entries.text:
*Rejected because:* a sync started in the source mid-clone would leave the copy holding files of two
revisions while its anchors name one, and its copied records would vouch for files they do not match. Holding
the locks throughout is the safe choice: the hold is minutes on APFS, and an estimated tens of minutes on Dev
Drive.

entries.title: lore\proposals\2026-10-31-copy-on-write-instance-clone.md
entries.text:
A command that gives a directory the user copied with `cp -c` or `cp --reflink` a new identity, registers
it and copies the source's anchors.

*Rejected because:* Lore cannot hold the source's repository lock across a copy it does not run. A copy
taken during a sync holds files of revision A while the anchors it adopts name revision B. Its copied
records vouch for the revision-A files' times, so the first scan skips them and status reports the tree as
clean at revision B while it is not.

entries.title: lore\proposals\2026-11-03-instance-ignore-rules.md
entries.text:
A user-level ignore file, read for every instance, as Git's `core.excludesFile`.

*Rejected because:* the rules describe one tree's build outputs, not the user's habits across repositories.
A path rule that suits one repository is wrong in another. It could be added later without changing this
design.

entries.title: lore\proposals\2026-11-03-instance-local-modified-time-records.md
entries.text:
The first upgraded command moves the instance's records into `.lore/` and zeroes them in the store.

*Rejected because:* for the instance measured here that is 1.1 million store reads and writes under the store
lock in one command, whatever that command was meant to do. Moving each record as its path is read
or changed spreads the same work across the commands that touch it.

entries.title: lore\proposals\2026-11-06-peer-read-fan-out.md
entries.text:
Every same-region node the topology reports, plus the local node, is a *member* with a *member id*. The
topology reports the local node's own member id as well as each peer's. A member id decides which slots a
node homes, so it must follow the node's cache: it stays the same while the machine and its cache can serve
the slots, and changes only when the node is a different machine. A valid member id is:

- **Unique among live members.** Two running nodes never share an id.
- **The same bytes everywhere.** The id a node reports for itself is exactly the id every peer sees for it.
- **Known locally at startup.** A node obtains its own id without asking another node or a service that
  issues ids, which would be a coordinator (Goal 7).
- **Independent of connections.** Rotating connection ids, reconnecting or changing peer connections leaves
  it unchanged.
- **Stable while the cache survives**, and **new when the machine changes**:

| Operation | Member id |
|---|---|
| Process restart or crash, config reload, connection id rotation | Same |
| Deploy of a new version on the same host | Same |
| Health check failure or short network partition | Same |
| Instance stop and start, or cache wiped, on the same host | Same, though the cache is empty |
| Job moved to a different host, instance replaced, node added | New |
| A second Lore Server process on the same host | Different from the first |

A node that keeps its id with an empty cache keeps its slots and reads the durable store for them until it
warms. Changing the id instead moves about twice as many slots for a similar number of durable reads, so an
id changes only with the machine. Reusing a departed node's id for its replacement is tolerated: the
replacement inherits the slots and starts cold. Each topology chooses where its member ids come from, as long
as they have these properties; Appendix A compares the candidate sources.

- The member list is the set the topology reports, not the set of peers a node managed to connect to.
  A home a node cannot reach counts as a failed home.
- A peer the topology reports without a member id is not a member: it keeps receiving writes but homes
  no slots.
- A peer whose member id equals the local node's is the local node, counted once. A topology that lists
  the local node among its peers, as the Consul source does unless `ignore_address` is set
  (`lore-hashicorp/src/consul/service_peer_discovery.rs`), therefore works unchanged.
- A node sends no home reads, and keeps today's fan-out, when its topology reports no member id for the
  local node, or when two different peers share an id. Such a node still answers home reads that other
  nodes send it.
- A topology composed of several sources reports a local member id when the sources that report one
  agree on it. Sources that report different local ids are a misconfiguration and leave home reads off.
- The topology source is the one input every node shares. When it is slow or unavailable, a node keeps
  routing on the last member list it received.

entries.title: lore\proposals\2026-11-06-peer-read-fan-out.md
entries.text:
A fragment's slot is a number taken from the last bytes of its hash, out of a fixed slot count of 16384.
The slot count never changes for a cluster, because changing it would move almost every fragment.

- **Why the last bytes.** The local immutable store groups and buckets fragments by the first two bytes
  of the hash (`lore-storage/src/local/fan_out.rs`), and each node needs an even spread inside its own
  store. Selecting the home by the last bytes keeps each node's local distribution even, provided the
  bytes of a BLAKE3 hash behave as independent (Risks and Assumptions).
- **Why the hash, not the address.** An address is a hash plus a context. Selecting the home from the
  hash alone sends every context of the same content to the same home, so the home can still report that
  it holds the content under another context or partition.
- **Why 16384.** A member's share of slots varies randomly around 1/N, and more slots make the variation
  smaller (Goal 3). Recomputing the assignment costs one hash per slot per member, about 75 ns each: about
  5 ms at four members and 12 ms at ten, timed with a release build on one core of an Apple M2 Max, once
  per membership change.

entries.title: lore\proposals\2026-11-06-peer-read-fan-out.md
entries.text:
Every node computes the owner of each slot from the member list alone; there is no stored table and no
coordinator. For each slot, each member gets a score: a fixed hash of its member id and the slot number.
The member with the highest score is the slot's *home*. This is rendezvous (highest random weight)
hashing applied per slot.

The scoring has the properties the goals need:

- **Agreement.** The hash is fixed, so nodes with the same member list compute the same home for every
  slot without exchanging messages.
- **Even shares.** Each member's score is in effect an independent draw, so each member wins about 1/N of
  the slots.
- **Minimal movement.** A member's score depends only on its own id and the slot. A member that joins
  takes only the slots where its score beats the current home: about 1/(N+1) of them, an equal share from
  each existing member. A member that leaves gives each of its slots to the member ranked second for that
  slot, and no other slot moves.
- **Known previous home.** When one member joins and nothing else changes, the member ranked second for
  each slot it took is the member that homed that slot before. Its score did not change, and it still
  outranks every other existing member.

A node recomputes the assignment whenever its member list changes. It computes the assignment whether or
not it sends home reads itself, so that it can serve them.

entries.title: lore\proposals\2026-11-06-peer-read-fan-out.md
entries.text:
On a local miss for an address:

- If the node is the address's home, it runs the home read path itself.
- Otherwise it sends one *home read* to the home. If the home fails, answers `SlowDown`, does not answer
  within the home read timeout, is not reachable, or rejects the request as unknown, the node reads the
  durable store itself.

The node caches what it receives, as it does today. A `query` batch splits by home: each part goes to
its own home, and a failed part falls back to the durable store for only its addresses.

Home reads travel over the same-region read peer connections, so a node with read replicas disabled
(`read_replicas_enabled = false`) sends none. With home reads on, the durable store delay
(`durable_store_delay_ms`) does not apply: the requester reads the durable store only after the home
fails.

Peer reads have no per-request timeout on the client today (`lore-server/src/store/replica.rs`). The
server refuses work beyond a per-connection limit, gives up on a request that waits too long for a handling
permit, and stops a request that exceeds its handling time limit, one hour by default, answering `SlowDown`
in each case (`lore-server/src/quic/stream_handler.rs`).
Neither bounds a read closely enough for a fallback, so this proposal adds a client timeout for home
reads.

entries.title: lore\proposals\2026-11-06-peer-read-fan-out.md
entries.text:
A home that does not hold a requested fragment:

1. asks the *runner-up*: the highest-ranked member for the slot other than itself, with one local-only
   peer read under its own timeout;
2. on a miss or failure, reads the durable store.

The home caches what it finds, then replies. The requester's home read timeout covers the runner-up
timeout plus a durable read.

- **Local-only peer reads never forward.** A peer answers them from its own cache
  (`lore-server/src/quic/replication_store_service/server.rs`).
- **One hop.** A node that receives a home read runs this path even when its own member list makes another
  node the home. A home read is never forwarded, so members that disagree cannot create a loop.
- **Shared lookups.** Concurrent `get` and `get_metadata` home reads for the same partition and address at
  one home share one lookup; a `query` part is looked up on its own, as `query` is at the requester today.
  A home's own client misses go through the requester path, so a home can briefly have both a
  home read and its own miss outstanding for one fragment.
- **Answers.** For `get`, the home's answer is final, including *not found*, because the home consulted the
  durable store last. For `query` and `get_metadata`, which report how strongly a store matches an address,
  the home merges the answers along its path and stops at the first full match or at the durable store's
  answer, the same stopping rule the composite store applies today.

entries.title: lore\proposals\2026-11-06-peer-read-fan-out.md
entries.text:
- **A member joins.** It homes about 1/(N+1) of the slots, taken equally from each existing member. Its first
  read of each such fragment goes to the runner-up, the previous home, so it warms from that member rather
  than the durable store. Existing members keep the copies they cached.
- **Several members join at once.** The runner-up of a moved slot can be another new member with an empty
  cache; those reads go to the durable store.
- **A member leaves or fails.** Each of its slots moves to the member ranked second. The new home holds the
  fragment if its own clients read it, or else asks its own runner-up, then the durable store. Until a node's
  member list drops the departed member, home reads to it fail and fall back to the durable store.
- **A member is replaced under the same member id.** It keeps the same slots and starts with an empty cache,
  which it fills through its read path.
- **Members disagree.** Nodes learn of membership changes at different times. During that window two nodes
  can compute different homes for a moved slot. The cost is extra peer requests or durable reads, never a
  wrong result, because the store is content-addressed.

entries.title: lore\proposals\2026-11-06-peer-read-fan-out.md
entries.text:
Writes go to the same write replicas as today, best effort. Today a write skips every peer if a topology
refresh holds the replica-list locks at that moment (`lore-revision/src/store/composite.rs`). With home
routing, a refresh in progress never causes a write to the fragment's home to be dropped: the node resolves
the home from its slot assignment and sends the write over whichever connection to the home exists, the one
from before the refresh or the one after it. Other peers keep today's behaviour.

entries.title: lore\proposals\2026-11-06-peer-read-fan-out.md
entries.text:
Home routing gives each node a role per slot, never a role for the cluster:

- **No coordinator.** Every node derives the slot assignment from its own member list. No node assigns slots,
  holds a table others depend on, or must be available for others to route.
- **Every node does every job.** Every node accepts client requests, acts as a requester, and serves every home
  read it receives. Being a home is a property of a slot, and every member homes about 1/N of them.
- **Correct answers from every node.** The store is content-addressed, so a fragment returned by any node is the
  right fragment. A *not found* from any node reflects the durable store.
- **No node answers better because of its role.** On a local miss, every node sends the read to the same home,
  which follows the same path, so every node receives the same answer from it. The home answers without a peer
  hop, so only its latency is better.
- **Losing a node loses no function.** When a node fails, its slots pass to their runner-ups and every remaining
  node keeps answering every request.

The match level that `query` and `get_metadata` report, and that `get` carries, can still differ between nodes,
as it does today. It differs in these cases:

- **A node's own cache.** Every node answers from its local cache before it sends a home read, and the caches
  differ. A node that holds the content under another context reports that weaker match without asking the home.
- **Fallback to the durable store.** A requester whose home read fails, times out or meets `SlowDown` gets the
  durable store's answer, which can be weaker than the home path's.
- **Member lists that differ.** While members disagree on the member list, or permanently if a node counts itself
  a member while its peers omit it, two nodes can route a slot to different homes.
- **Nodes on today's fan-out.** A node with `home_reads` off, without a local member id, or with duplicate peer
  ids merges every peer's answer as today.
- **Timeout settings that differ** between nodes change when each falls back.

In every case the fragment content is the same, and the difference is in the hint that lets a put become a copy.

entries.title: lore\proposals\2026-11-06-peer-read-fan-out.md
entries.text:
Keep asking every peer on a miss, now that peer hits are cached.

*Rejected because:* every remaining miss still sends a request to every peer and receives a reply from every peer
that holds the fragment, so peer traffic per miss still grows with the number of nodes, and a new node still pulls
from every peer.

entries.title: lore\proposals\2026-11-06-peer-read-fan-out.md
entries.text:
After the runner-up, ask each other member in turn before the durable store.

*Rejected because:* a cold miss then waits for up to N−1 peer round trips before the durable read. Since every node
caches what it reads and the home is where requesters go first, a fragment missing at both the home and the
runner-up is less likely to be held by a third member than to be held by none.

entries.title: lore\proposals\2026-11-06-peer-read-fan-out.md
entries.text:
Keep an explicit slot-to-node table in a shared store such as Consul's key-value store, edited by one leader that
moves the fewest slots needed for an exact split.

*Rejected because:* it introduces a leader, which Goal 7 rules out, along with locking and a rebalance procedure,
for a gain of a few percent in balance; a stalled leader would leave a new node without slots. The data on each
node is a cache, so a derived assignment's statistical balance costs little.

entries.title: lore\proposals\2026-11-06-peer-read-fan-out.md
entries.text:
Place each member at several positions on a hash ring and give each position the range up to the next.

*Rejected because:* the virtual-node positions form a derived table of the same kind as the slot assignment, with
more entries per member for comparable balance, and the previous owner of a range is a neighbour on the ring rather
than a single, directly computed runner-up.

entries.title: lore\proposals\2026-11-06-peer-read-fan-out.md
entries.text:
No topology reports a node's own id today, and the peer ids they report differ:

| Topology | Peer id today | Stable | Node knows its own |
|---|---|---|---|
| Consul | The Consul node id (`lore-hashicorp/src/consul/service_peer_discovery.rs`) | Yes, per host; the Consul agent keeps it in its data directory | No |
| Fixed | A label built from locality, address and port (`lore-server/src/topology/fixed.rs`) | Yes, while the configuration is unchanged | No |
| Rotating | A random value on every rotation (`lore-server/src/topology/rotating_id_fixed.rs`) | No, by design | No |

Three candidate sources, measured against the properties in Members and member ids:

| Property | Advertised address and port | Consul node id | Configured id |
|---|---|---|---|
| Unique among live members | Yes; the port separates processes on one host | No for two processes on one host | Only if operators assign it correctly |
| The same bytes everywhere | Yes, if every node uses the service address its peers see | Yes | Yes, if advertised to peers |
| Known locally at startup | Yes; deployments that set `ignore_address` already supply it | Needs a query to the local Consul agent, or injection at deploy time | Yes |
| Independent of connections | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| Same across restart and redeploy on one host | Yes, while the address and port do not change | Yes | Yes |
| New on replacement, move or scale-out | Yes | Yes | Only if operators issue a new one |
| Works in every topology | Yes | Consul only | Yes, with new configuration in each |
| Changes when it should not | An operator changes the address or port | The Consul agent's data directory is lost | Operator error |

- **Advertised address and port** meets every property without new infrastructure. Every node must use the service
  address its peers see; the Consul source today filters on the node address but builds peers from the service
  address, and the two can differ.
- **Consul node id** is already the Consul peer id, but fails uniqueness for two processes on one host, works only with
  Consul, and needs each node to discover its own id.
- **A configured id** meets every property only if operators never duplicate or reuse it by mistake, and needs new
  configuration and a discovery field in every deployment.

entries.title: lore\proposals\README.md
entries.text:
These apply across every section.

- **Active voice.** Write "this proposal rejects approach X", not "approach X was rejected"; "Lore writes the new version", not "the new version is written by Lore". Past-participle adjectives ("the upgraded client", "the proposed design") are fine.
- **Public citations.** LEPs are public. Support every factual claim either with a public link (RFC, code path in the Lore tree, a public ADR, an upstream project doc) or by capturing the relevant detail inline. Internal-only resources (internal code reviews, JIRA tickets, Slack threads, internal wikis) can't be shared externally and shouldn't be included in the LEP — they don't substitute for support in the body.
- **Discussion link.** The `discussion` frontmatter field is optional. When set, it links to a public discussion of the proposal, such as a public pull request or issue. Leave it out rather than link an internal review or thread.
- **Ground every claim.** If you can't back something up with research, prior discussion, or the proposal itself, leave it out rather than filling space.
- **One decision per proposal.** Propose one change that can be accepted on its own. When parts of a proposal have their own goals, risks, and compatibility surface, write a proposal for each, so that accepting one doesn't decide the others. A change to an accepted proposal is an amendment to it, as [Lifecycle](#lifecycle) describes.
- **Lore terms.** Use the terms the [glossary](../glossary.md) defines, in the sense it defines them. Don't give a defined term a second meaning.

entries.title: lore\reference\lore-cli-commands.md
entries.text:
Show current repository status.

Reports the staged revision (if any) and the files currently marked dirty. No filesystem walk runs by default — pass
`--scan` to walk the filesystem and refresh dirty flags. See `lore status --help` (top-level alias) for the full
workflow.

**Usage:** `lore repository status [OPTIONS] [PATH]...`

###### **Arguments:**

* `<PATH>` — Optional paths in repository

###### **Options:**

* `--scan` — Walk the filesystem under the given paths and reconcile every file against the current revision.

  Detected modifications, adds, and deletes are marked dirty; stale dirty flags are cleared. The refreshed flags are
  persisted in the staged state so subsequent `lore stage` and `lore status` calls see an accurate picture without
  rescanning.

  Without `--scan`, status reports only what is currently tracked: the staged revision (if any) plus files already
  marked dirty. Mark files individually with `lore dirty` for targeted updates, or pass `--scan` here for bulk
  reconciliation.
* `--check-dirty` — Verify already-dirty files against the filesystem without a full scan.

  Each file currently marked dirty is re-checked: one whose on-disk content still matches the tracked revision (same
  size, and same content when the modification time differs) has its dirty flag cleared and is dropped from the report,
  unless it is also staged. Adds, moves, copies, and deletes are always reported. The refreshed flags are persisted, so
  this requires write access.
* `--reset` — Drop the existing staged anchor before computing status. Combine with --scan to scan from a clean slate
* `--revision-only` — Only show revision info, skip all diffs
* `--count` — Count directories and files (staged state if present, else current revision; view-filtered)
* `--targets <file>` — Path to a targets file

entries.title: lore\reference\lore-cli-commands.md
entries.text:
Create a repository in the given directory

**Usage:** `lore repository create [OPTIONS] [url]`

###### **Arguments:**

* `<url>` — URL of repository. With --offline this is the repository name instead, and may be omitted to name it after
  the current directory

###### **Options:**

* `--description <description>` — Optional description of repository
* `--id <id>` — Optional ID of repository
* `--vfs <VFS>` — Virtual File System type. When not 'none', creates a VFS as the repository directory, over a shared store as if --use-shared-store were given

  Default value: `none`

  Possible values:
    - `none`:
      No virtual file system; files are materialized directly on disk
    - `default`:
      Use whichever VFS system is preferred based on the user's system
    - `swfs`:
      Use Epic's Split Write File System as the Virtual File System. An SWFS instance keeps its content in the shared
      store made for its remote, so it needs a reachable remote: it cannot be created offline, or for a repository with
      no remote

* `--use-shared-store` — Use the shared store rather than create a local immutable store. A VFS always does
* `--shared-store-path <SHARED_STORE_PATH>` — Use this path rather than the system default as the shared store location

entries.title: lore\reference\lore-cli-commands.md
entries.text:
Clone a remote repository into the given path

A clone needs the remote, so `--offline` does not keep it from connecting: it prepares the clone for working offline
instead. With it, as with `--cache`, a clone that writes its files caches every file metadata block of the cloned
revision, which staging and committing write to, so both work without the remote, and fails if it cannot. A bare or
virtual clone writes no files and reads them from the remote when a command needs them.

**Usage:** `lore repository clone [OPTIONS] <url> [path]`

###### **Arguments:**

* `<url>` — URL of repository
* `<path>` — Path to clone into

###### **Options:**

* `--view <view>` — Optional client side view filter file
* `--revision <revision>` — Optional revision to sync
* `--branch <branch>` — Optional branch to sync (shorthand for a full revision specifier)
* `--bare` — Clone without files, only fetch latest revision tree
* `--direct-file-write` — Write directly to the destination file instead of write to a temporary file and move into
  place
* `--vfs <VFS>` — Virtual File System type. When not 'none', creates a VFS as the repository directory, over a shared store as if --use-shared-store were given

  Default value: `none`

  Possible values:
    - `none`:
      No virtual file system; files are materialized directly on disk
    - `default`:
      Use whichever VFS system is preferred based on the user's system
    - `swfs`:
      Use Epic's Split Write File System as the Virtual File System. An SWFS instance keeps its content in the shared
      store made for its remote, so it needs a reachable remote: it cannot be created offline, or for a repository with
      no remote

* `--layer <repository>` — Layer to add
* `--layer-metadata <key>` — Metadata key to link layer revisions with
* `--prefetch <file>` — Access recording whose paths a virtual clone warms in the background (one path per line, directories ending with `/`)
* `--use-shared-store` — Use the shared store rather than create a local immutable store. A VFS always does
* `--shared-store-path <SHARED_STORE_PATH>` — Use this path rather than the system default as the shared store location
* `--no-tracking` — Clone without local repository tracking (memory-only stores)
* `--root-file <path>` — Root files for dependency-based selective clone (only clone these files and their dependencies).
  A root file inside a link is skipped
* `--dependency-tag <tag>` — Tags to filter dependencies by during dependency-based clone
* `--dependency-recursive` — Follow transitive dependencies recursively during dependency-based clone
* `--dependency-depth-limit <depth>` — Maximum dependency traversal depth (0 means unlimited)

  Default value: `0`

entries.title: lore\reference\lore-cli-commands.md
entries.text:
Instance management

**Usage:** `lore repository instance <COMMAND>`

###### **Subcommands:**

* `list` — List all registered instances for this repository
* `prune` — Remove stale instance entries: paths that no longer exist, paths that hold no revision, and paths that now
  hold a different instance. An SWFS instance is kept while its `.lore` remains in the global data directory, even when
  it is not mounted
* `delete` — Delete the current instance: unmount (if SWFS or a virtual clone), deregister from mutable store, and
  delete associated directories
* `move` — Move the current instance to a new path
* `clone` — Clone the current instance to a new path as an instance of its own, on the same revision, branch and staged
  state. The clone shares the instance's data blocks, and is refused where the destination's filesystem or volume
  cannot share them unless --allow-copy is given. The instance must use a shared store and not be a virtual clone, and
  the path must not be inside another instance. While the clone runs, commands on the instance, and commands from
  other processes on every instance over the store, wait for it where they open the store. An instance delete waits
  too, since it opens the store to deregister the instance before it removes any file. An instance move renames the
  instance before it opens the store, so a move makes the clone fail, or on Windows is refused while the clone lists
  one of its directories

entries.title: lore\reference\lore-cli-commands.md
entries.text:
Clone the current instance to a new path as an instance of its own, on the same revision, branch and staged state. The
clone shares the instance's data blocks, and is refused where the destination's filesystem or volume cannot share them
unless --allow-copy is given. The instance must use a shared store and not be a virtual clone, and the path must not be
inside another instance. While the clone runs, commands on the instance, and commands from other processes on every
instance over the store, wait for it where they open the store. An instance delete waits too, since it opens the store
to deregister the instance before it removes any file. An instance move renames the instance before it opens the
store, so a move makes the clone fail, or on Windows is refused while the clone lists one of its directories

**Usage:** `lore repository instance clone [OPTIONS] <target-path>`

###### **Arguments:**

* `<target-path>` — Path to create the clone at; it must not exist, and must be on the instance's volume for the clone
  to share its data blocks

###### **Options:**

* `--allow-copy` — Copy the instance's files where the clone cannot share their data blocks, rather than refusing. A
  copy takes as long as writing every file, and commands wait for it as they wait for every clone

entries.title: lore\reference\lore-cli-commands.md
entries.text:
Stage changes for commit.

Directory paths (including `.`) stage only files already marked dirty under that directory; clean or unmarked files are
skipped. Mark files first with `lore file dirty` (or `lore status --scan` to reconcile dirty flags in bulk), or pass
`--scan` here to walk the filesystem and stage in one pass.

Specific file paths are checked against the filesystem and staged if content differs from the current revision,
regardless of their dirty flag.

`--scan` walks the filesystem under the given paths, marks every detected modification/add/delete dirty, and stages them
in one step.

**Usage:** `lore file stage [OPTIONS] <paths|--targets <file>>
       stage [OPTIONS] <COMMAND>`

###### **Subcommands:**

* `move` — Move or rename a file or directory
* `merge` — Stage as a merge

###### **Arguments:**

* `<paths>` — Any number of paths or files

###### **Options:**

* `--case <case>` — Case change handling

  Possible values:
    - `error`:
      Generate error on case mismatch
    - `keep`:
      Keep current case in repository (update file system)
    - `rename`:
      Rename case in repository (keep file system)

* `--scan` — Walk the filesystem under the given paths to detect modified, added, and deleted files.

  Detected changes are marked dirty and staged in a single pass. Use this when changes were made externally (without
  going through `lore dirty`), or to recover after losing track of dirty state. Equivalent in effect to running
  `lore status --scan` followed by `lore stage`, but performed in one traversal.

  Without `--scan`, directory staging stages only files already marked dirty under that directory — mark them first with
  `lore dirty <paths>`, or run `lore status --scan` to reconcile dirty flags across a tree. Single-file stage paths are
  always checked against the filesystem regardless of this flag.
* `--targets <file>` — Path to a targets file containing all the paths to all files

entries.title: lore\reference\lore-cli-commands.md
entries.text:
Mark files as dirty so they show up in `lore status` and get picked up by directory-scoped `lore stage` (no content is
read or staged).

Use when files were changed externally and you want to notify Lore of specific paths without performing a full
filesystem walk. For bulk reconciliation across a tree, prefer `lore status --scan` or `lore stage --scan`.

**Usage:** `lore file dirty [OPTIONS] [paths]... [COMMAND]`

###### **Subcommands:**

* `move` — Mark a file as moved (dirty)
* `copy` — Mark a file as copied (dirty)

###### **Arguments:**

* `<paths>` — Any number of paths or files

###### **Options:**

* `--targets <file>` — Path to a targets file containing all the paths to all files

entries.title: lore\reference\lore-cli-commands.md
entries.text:
Reset changes to a path or file to the current revision, discarding your local changes

**Usage:** `lore file reset [OPTIONS] <paths|--targets <file>>`

###### **Arguments:**

* `<paths>` — Any number of paths or files

###### **Options:**

* `--purge` — Delete every file the revision does not hold within the view: untracked files, whatever the ignore file
  says, and files the view excludes. Nested repositories stay. With `--force` the view is not applied, and the files it
  excludes are restored
* `--targets <file>` — Path to a targets file containing all the paths to all files
* `--revision <revision>` — Revision to reset files to
* `--last-merged-from <branch>` — If given, the files will be reset to the last point of merge from this branch, or the
  branch point from this branch if no merge has been performed
* `--mine` — Reset to the version this branch held going into that merge rather than the version the conflict was
  resolved with
* `--theirs` — Reset to the version the merged branch brought in rather than the version the conflict was resolved with

entries.title: lore\reference\lore-cli-commands.md
entries.text:
List revisions of a file

**Usage:** `lore file history [OPTIONS] <PATH> [LENGTH]`

###### **Arguments:**

* `<PATH>` — File path to get revisions for

###### **Options:**

* `--branch <branch>` — Show branch revisions

* `--oneline` — Output each revision on one line only

entries.title: lore\reference\lore-cli-commands.md
entries.text:
Attribute each line of a file to the revision that last changed it

**Usage:** `lore file audit [OPTIONS] <PATH>`

###### **Arguments:**

* `<PATH>` — File path to attribute

###### **Options:**

* `--revision <revision>` — Revision to read the file at: a revision signature, `[branch]@<number>`, `[branch]@LATEST`
  or `<branch>@<hash>`, optionally followed by `~<count>` to step back that many parents. Without it the file is read at
  the revision the instance is synced to, and the file on disk is accounted for
* `--max-revisions <n>` — Comparisons of the file's predecessor chain to make, 0 for no limit.

  This bounds the work, not the number of revisions the answer can name. A comparison against the revision that added
  the file resolves that revision too, and a comparison at a revision that left the file alone resolves none, so the
  rows reported can be one more or one fewer than the bound allows.

  Default value: `100`
* `--ignore-space-at-eol` — Treat lines that differ only in trailing whitespace as unchanged

  On by default, unlike `lore file diff`: attribution asks who wrote a line, and trailing-space or line-ending churn
  does not answer that. Turn it off with --no-ignore-space-at-eol.
* `--no-ignore-space-at-eol` — Count a line that differs only in trailing whitespace as changed
* `--ignore-space-change` — Collapse runs of internal whitespace to a single space before comparing

  Leaves a reindented line with the revision that wrote its text.

entries.title: lore\reference\lore-cli-commands.md
entries.text:
Show differences between two revisions of a file

**Usage:** `lore file diff [OPTIONS] [paths]...`

###### **Arguments:**

* `<paths>` — Any number of paths or files

###### **Options:**

* `--source <revision_source>` — Optional signature of the source revision to diff from, by default the current revision
* `--target <revision_target>` — Optional signature of the target revision to diff to, by default the current file
  system state
* `--diff3` — If given, produce three-way merge output with conflict markers instead of a two-way unified diff
* `-U`, `--context <n>` — Number of unchanged context lines to show around each hunk

  Default value: `3`
* `--ignore-space-at-eol` — Treat lines that differ only in trailing whitespace as unchanged
* `--ignore-space-change` — Collapse runs of internal whitespace to a single space before comparing
* `--targets <file>` — Path to a targets file containing all the paths to all files

entries.title: lore\reference\lore-cli-commands.md
entries.text:
Authenticate the CLI

**Usage:** `lore auth login [OPTIONS] [remote-url]`

###### **Arguments:**

* `<remote-url>` — Server URL

###### **Options:**

* `--token-type <TOKEN_TYPE>` — Token type for non-interactive login (e.g. "api-key", "eg1", "lore")
* `--token <TOKEN>` — Token value for non-interactive login (requires --token-type). Read from `LORE_TOKEN` when omitted.
  Unsafe: a value given here is visible to other users in the process table and is kept in the shell history
* `--client-id <CLIENT_ID>` — Log in as this confidential client registered with the identity provider, authenticating
  with its client secret
* `--client-secret <CLIENT_SECRET>` — Client secret for --client-id. Read from `LORE_CLIENT_SECRET` when omitted. Unsafe:
  a value given here is visible to other users in the process table and is kept in the shell history
* `--auth-url <AUTH_URL>` — Auth service URL with scheme (e.g. `ucs-auth://auth.google.com`). Required when logging in
  with `--token` outside a repository without a remote-url
* `--no-browser` — Avoid opening a browser to login
* `--reuse-session` — Keep the stored login instead of logging in again while its session is valid
