entries.title: lore\reference\lore-cli-config.md
entries.text:
| Variable | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `LORE_SERVICE_SOCKET` | Names the socket a service listens on. Processes sharing a value share a service; processes with different values get one each. |

Every service belonging to a user answers on the same socket by default, which is what makes one service serve every command that user runs. It is also why a test suite, or a second checkout, would otherwise take over the service already running: stopping and starting one affects whatever else was using it.

Set `LORE_SERVICE_SOCKET` to give a group of processes a service of their own. The value names a single file, not a path — anything containing a path separator is refused in favour of the default rather than honoured, since the socket's directory is chosen for being private to your user and a path could move it somewhere with weaker permissions.

```bash
export LORE_SERVICE_SOCKET=lore_service-my-checkout
```

The Python test suite sets this per run, so running it leaves a service you have running alone.

entries.title: lore\reference\lore-cli-config.md
entries.text:
Override the `[store]` defaults to give this repository a larger local immutable store and a longer eviction delay:

```toml
remote_url = "lore://127.0.0.1:41337/my-project"
identity = "alex@google.com"

[store]
max_size = 53687091200    # 50 GiB
max_capacity = 10000000   # fragments
eviction_delay = 60
```

A repository created by `lore repository create` or `lore clone` already has every `[store]` field but `verify_write` and `cache_payloads` populated at its written default, so you edit values that are already present. The `[store]` example above is shown trimmed for clarity.

entries.title: lore\reference\lore-server-config.md
entries.text:
The `[server]` table and its sub-tables configure the network endpoints, graceful-shutdown behavior, and the disk space check on the local stores.

| Field | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `server.connection_close_timeout_seconds` | `5` | Seconds to wait for open connections to close after a shutdown signal. |
| `server.runtime_shutdown_timeout_seconds` | `25` | Seconds to wait for the async runtime to shut down after connections close. Accepts the alias `shutdown_delay_seconds`. |
| `server.trust_unsigned_identity` | `false` | Without `[server.auth]`, take the caller's identity from an unsigned bearer token on gRPC, HTTP and QUIC. See [Unsigned identity](#unsigned-identity). The server refuses to start if it is set beside `[server.auth]`. |
| `server.upstream_connections` | `4` | Storage connections the server opens to the [upstream](../glossary.md#upstream) of a `remote` immutable or mutable store for each identity it authenticates there as (see [Remote store mode](#remote-store-mode)), from `1` to `10`; `0` reads as `1`. The connections belong to the upstream and the identity, not to a repository: every repository the server reaches there as that identity shares them, as do its QUIC, gRPC and socket handlers. |

entries.title: lore\reference\lore-server-config.md
entries.text:
`[server.local_store_monitor]` configures the periodic check of the disk space left to the local stores (see [Store settings](#store-settings)). Only stores the server writes at are watched, so a `[local]` block left in a remote deployment's configuration is ignored, as is a composite immutable tier that names a path other than the first local tier's — every local tier is handed the store the first one creates.

| Field | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `check_interval_seconds` | `30` | Seconds between checks. `0` turns the check off. |
| `low_space_threshold_bytes` | `10737418240` | Warn while free space on a volume holding a local store is below this (10 GiB). |

The reading is taken per volume, not per store: stores sharing a filesystem are checked once and named together in a single warning. The first check runs at startup, so a server starting on a full volume says so immediately. A store path that matches no mounted filesystem is warned about once and goes unmonitored until a mount covers it again.

At startup the server also reports where each local store lands, warning when the configuration names no path, when the path is inside a system temporary directory (see [Zero-config defaults](#zero-config-defaults)), and when a composite tier names a path nothing is written at.

entries.title: lore\reference\lore-server-config.md
entries.text:
`[server.grpc_public_services]` holds one block per service the public gRPC endpoint can register, plus `forwarded_requests`.

Every service block accepts `enabled` and a `general` namespace. A block may
also define service-specific fields. A `general` field affects only the
services named in its description:

| Field | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `enabled` | `true` | Whether the public router registers this service. Set `false` and every RPC on it answers `UNIMPLEMENTED`. |
| `general.max_encoding_message_size` | unset | Maximum encoded gRPC response size in bytes. When unset, the gRPC framework default applies. Honored by `lock_service`. |

Use `lock_service.general.max_encoding_message_size` instead of
`lock_service.max_encoding_message_size`, which current servers ignore. During
a mixed-version rollout, set both paths. Legacy servers read the direct key;
current servers read the key beneath `general`. Remove the direct key after all
servers are upgraded.

#### Selecting services

An absent block means enabled. A present block without `enabled` also means
enabled. Restrict a deployment by disabling every service it must not serve:

| Block | Registers |
| --- | --- |
| `admin_service` | `urc.rpc.AdminService` (`ServerInfo`, `Obliterate`) |
| `storage_service` | `urc.rpc.StorageService` and `lore.storage.v1.StorageService` |
| `revision_service` | `urc.rpc.RevisionService` and `lore.revision.v1.RevisionService` |
| `repository_service` | `urc.rpc.RepositoryService` and `lore.repository.v1.RepositoryService` |
| `environment_service` | `urc.rpc.EnvironmentService` and `lore.environment.v1.EnvironmentService` |
| `thin_client_service` | `lore.thin_client.v1.ThinClientService`. Every RPC it serves is a read. |
| `lock_service` | `urc.lock.LockService`. Also requires `[lock_store]` at a mode other than `none`. |
| `notification_service` | `lore.notification.NotificationService`. Registers for local notification mode, the default when `[notification]` is absent. Notification plugins provide a sender but do not register this public service. |

One block gates a whole proto family. The legacy `urc.rpc` services are not
read-only shadows of their `v1` twins. They carry `BranchPush`,
`RepositoryCreate`, and `RepositoryDelete`.

Each flag is a scalar, so it is also settable from the environment:

```shell
LORE__SERVER__GRPC_PUBLIC_SERVICES__STORAGE_SERVICE__ENABLED=false
```

Disabling every service is legal. The process starts, and the public gRPC
listener answers every RPC with `UNIMPLEMENTED`. The same result occurs when
only `lock_service` is enabled without a store, or only `notification_service`
is enabled with a notification plugin. An empty effective set logs a warning:
`No public gRPC services registered; every RPC on this listener will answer
UNIMPLEMENTED`.

Unknown keys are ignored, as elsewhere in the settings. A misspelled block or
key therefore leaves the service registered. Verify the effective set in the
startup log.

The startup message `Registered public gRPC services` lists the services that
the router registered. Its `authenticated` field reports whether `[server.auth]`
is active. The effective set can differ from the configured set because
`lock_service` requires a store and `notification_service` requires local mode.

For example, a read-only thin-client deployment disables every other service:

```toml
# Enabled by default; written out so the file states what the process serves.
[server.grpc_public_services.thin_client_service]
enabled = true

[server.grpc_public_services.admin_service]
enabled = false

[server.grpc_public_services.storage_service]
enabled = false

# ... revision_service, repository_service, environment_service,
#     lock_service, notification_service
```

`lore-server/config/thin.example.toml` is a complete example. It contains the
exclusions above, disables the QUIC and HTTP listeners, and points both stores
at a separate full server so the process keeps no repository copy.

entries.title: lore\reference\lore-server-config.md
entries.text:
`[immutable_store.local]` and `[mutable_store.local]` configure the on-disk local stores. The mutable store accepts only `path` and `flush_delay_seconds`; the immutable store accepts the full set below.

| Field | Default | Applies to | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `path` | derived `<temp>/lore-server` | both | Filesystem location for the store. When empty, the server derives a path under the system temporary directory at startup (ephemeral — see [Zero-config defaults](#zero-config-defaults)). |
| `flush_delay_seconds` | `10` | both | Seconds between background flushes to disk. In the immutable store, index writes pending after a capacity eviction pass are also spread across this interval, group by group, except in maintenance mode, where they are written as the pass ends. If the server stops before a group's writes reach disk, the entries evicted from that group are back when it restarts. |
| `max_capacity` | none | immutable | Maximum number of entries before eviction. |
| `max_size` | none | immutable | Maximum total store size in bytes before background compaction reclaims space. Compaction rewrites a group's packfiles only once at least 10% of their bytes are no longer referenced. |
| `eviction_delay` | none | immutable | Interval in milliseconds between eviction passes. Defaults to 10 s when unset. |
| `compaction_delay` | none | immutable | Interval in milliseconds between compaction passes. Defaults to 24 h when unset. |
| `target_capacity_percentage` | `70` | immutable | Capacity-utilization target (percent) that eviction reclaims down to. Applies only when `max_capacity` is set; 0 or ≥100 is treated as `70`. |
| `target_size_percentage` | `70` | immutable | Size-utilization target (percent) that compaction reclaims down to. Applies only when `max_size` is set; 0 or ≥100 is treated as `70`. |
| `compaction_parallel_groups` | `8` | immutable | Number of compaction groups processed in parallel. |

> [!NOTE]
> The `composite` mode layers a local cache tier over a durable plugin tier (for example, a local cache in front of S3). It reads `[immutable_store.composite.local]` and `[immutable_store.composite.durable]`, where the durable tier names a plugin mode such as `aws`, or `remote` (see [Remote store mode](#remote-store-mode)). Composite and replicated store internals are out of scope here.

The lock store's `local` mode takes no sub-table — it uses an in-process, in-memory lock store (a single in-memory map) with no fields to configure. Because it lives entirely within one server process, it coordinates locks only on that node; distributed locking across a multi-node cluster requires a plugin backend such as `aws` (DynamoDB).

entries.title: lore\reference\lore-server-config.md
entries.text:
The `remote` mode keeps a store at another Lore server, the upstream, which the server reaches as a client does: the immutable store reads and writes content there, and the mutable store loads and stores mutable keys there, but lists none. `[immutable_store] mode = "remote"` reads `[immutable_store.remote]`, `[mutable_store] mode = "remote"` reads `[mutable_store.remote]`, and a composite store's durable tier in `remote` mode reads `[immutable_store.composite.durable.remote]`. The server refuses to start in `remote` mode without the table. How many storage connections it opens to the upstream follows `server.upstream_connections` (see [Server and endpoint settings](#server-and-endpoint-settings)).

| Field | Default | Applies to | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `remote_url` | required | both | URL of the upstream as a client names it, without a repository, for example `lores://lore.google.com:41337`. |
| `verify` | `false` | immutable | Whether the store checks each payload the upstream serves against its address, decoding and hashing it. When `false`, the store trusts the upstream and checks only a payload's sizes. Either way, a client checks each payload it fetches from the server against its address, except a client that trusts its remote (`--trust-remote`, or `trust_remote` or `skip_verify` through the C API), which checks only the sizes. A client that finds a payload corrupt asks the server to heal it: the server drops its own copy only if that copy is corrupt, and asks the upstream to heal only where its own copy was corrupt or missing. |
| `auth_url` | none | immutable | Despite its name, the identity the store authenticates at the upstream as, not a URL. The server uses the login stored for that identity in the token store of the user it runs as. When unset, the store uses the first identity stored there that the upstream accepts. The `remote` mutable store ignores the field and always uses that first identity. |

```toml
[mutable_store]
mode = "remote"

[mutable_store.remote]
remote_url = "lores://lore.google.com:41337"
```

entries.title: lore\reference\lore-server-config.md
entries.text:
`[topology.rotating_id_fixed]` is `fixed` with periodically rotating peer IDs. It takes the same `peers` array plus a required `rotation_interval_seconds`.

```toml
[topology]
provider = "rotating_id_fixed"

[topology.rotating_id_fixed]
rotation_interval_seconds = 300
peers = [{ address = "192.168.1.10", port = 41340, locality = "SameRegion" }]
```

entries.title: lore\reference\lore-server-config.md
entries.text:
Five kinds of backend can be supplied by a plugin, each chosen by a different field:

| Plugin kind | Selector | Built-in alternatives |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Immutable store | `immutable_store.mode` | `local`, `composite`, `replicated`, `remote` |
| Mutable store | `mutable_store.mode` | `local`, `remote` |
| Lock store | `lock_store.mode` | `local`, `none` |
| Topology | `topology.provider` | `none`, `fixed`, `rotating_id_fixed`, `composite` |
| Notification | `notification.mode` | `local` |

When a selector names a plugin rather than a built-in, the server hands that plugin its `[plugins.<name>]` table as raw configuration and lets the plugin parse it. The field names and defaults of `[plugins.<name>]` are therefore owned by the plugin — and by the binary that compiles it in — not by `loreserver`. If no plugin of that name is registered, startup fails with `PluginNotFound`; a malformed plugin table fails with `PluginConfigError`; and a plugin that starts but cannot reach its backend fails with `PluginInitError`.

entries.title: lore\reference\lore-server-config.md
entries.text:
Hooks run custom logic at points in the server lifecycle. Each hook is configured in its own `[hooks.<name>]` table. Every hook table has an `enabled` flag (default `false`) plus fields specific to that hook.

Hooks fire at these points:

- **`BranchPush`** — before a branch push is committed.
- **`BranchCreate`** — before a new branch is created.
- **`BranchDelete`** — before a branch is deleted.
- **`RepositoryCreate`** — before a new repository is created.
- **`Obliterate`** — before content is obliterated.

A hook's pre-handler runs before the operation, and the operation waits for it. A pre-handler still running after 1 second, or after the timeout the hook sets for itself, is cancelled and the operation fails with `UNAVAILABLE`, so the client can retry. On the v1 `BranchPush`, `BranchCreate`, and `BranchDelete` RPCs, a pre-handler sees the branch name and whether the caller is a service account.

A hook can veto an operation by returning an error, log or audit it, or trigger an external notification. The example below sketches a compliance hook that denies pushes to protected branch patterns and posts to a webhook on failure. It is illustrative — `deny_patterns`, `allowed_users`, and `webhook_url` are fields a *custom* compliance hook would define; the stock `loreserver` ships no such hook (see note below):

```toml
# Illustrative only — requires a custom "compliance" hook compiled in.
[hooks.compliance]
enabled = true
deny_patterns = ["^release/.*$", "^protected/.*$"]
allowed_users = ["admin", "release-bot"]
webhook_url = "https://compliance.google.com/notify"
```

| Field | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `enabled` | Whether the hook is active. Defaults to `false`. |
| Hook-specific fields | Each hook defines its own fields — for example `deny_patterns`, `allowed_users`, and `webhook_url` for a compliance hook, or per-event webhook URLs for a notification hook. |

> [!NOTE]
> The base `loreserver` binary registers no hooks. A `[hooks.<name>]` table is matched by name against hooks compiled into the binary: a *disabled* table for an unknown hook is ignored, but an **enabled** table naming a hook that isn't compiled in aborts server startup. Custom hooks implement the `Hook` and `HookFactory` traits in Rust and are wired in by `build.rs` at compile time (the registry is populated at startup).

entries.title: lore\reference\lore-server-config.md
entries.text:
`[telemetry.metrics]` and `[telemetry.traces]` ship in `default.toml` with the defaults below.

`[telemetry.metrics]`:

| Field | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `export_interval_millis` | `30000` | Interval in milliseconds between samples of the async (Tokio) runtime metrics. |
| `sample_interval_millis` | `10000` | Interval in milliseconds at which the OTLP reader exports metrics to the collector; also paces local-store memory-stats reporting. |

`[telemetry.traces]`:

| Field | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `sample_rate` | `0.05` | Fraction of traces sampled. |
| `sample_rate_low_tier` | `0.001` | Sampling fraction applied to low-tier (high-volume) traces. |
| `service_name` | none | Service name reported on exported traces. Falls back to `lore` when unset. |

> [!NOTE]
> Both sample rates must fall within `[0.0, 1.0]` inclusive, or the server refuses to start with a configuration error.

entries.title: lore\reference\lore-server-config.md
entries.text:
```bash
loreserver
```

Starts a single-node server from the built-in defaults: an ephemeral self-signed certificate, a store under `<temp>/lore-server`, and the presigned URL feature disabled. Everything is local — the certificate is regenerated on each start, and the store lives in the OS temp directory, which a reboot can clear. For trying Lore out, not for keeping data.

entries.title: lore\reference\lore-server-config.md
entries.text:
Create a config directory with a `local.toml` that pins the stores to a fixed path and references real certificates:

```toml
# ./config/local.toml
[server.quic.certificate]
cert_file = "./cert.pem"
pkey_file = "./key.pem"

[immutable_store.local]
path = "/var/lib/lore/store"
flush_delay_seconds = 10

[mutable_store.local]
path = "/var/lib/lore/store"
flush_delay_seconds = 10

[topology]
provider = "none"
```

```bash
loreserver --config ./config
```

The `local.toml` overlay overrides the defaults, so the stores persist at `/var/lib/lore/store` across restarts.

entries.title: lore\reference\lore-server-config.md
entries.text:
```bash
loreserver --config /etc/lore/config --env dev
```

Layers `/etc/lore/config/dev.toml` over the built-in defaults, then `/etc/lore/config/local.toml`. A missing `dev.toml` is skipped, so this is safe even when only `local.toml` exists. The same selection works through environment variables: `LORE_ENV=dev LORE_CONFIG_PATH=/etc/lore/config loreserver`.

entries.title: lore\release-notes.md
entries.text:
- `lore-server`: a storage copy reports a slow-down from the store as `SlowDown` over QUIC and `RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED` over gRPC, rather than as an internal error. The legacy `urc.rpc` gRPC get, put and copy streams report a slow-down as `RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED` as well
- When a storage copy receives a slow-down response, the client backs off and retries the copy, as it does an upload. If the server is still throttling when the retries run out, the client doesn't upload the payload. A write keeps it locally without marking it durable, as when an upload runs out of retries, and `lore push` fails with a slow-down error. The client used to upload the full payload straight away
- gRPC connections over TLS fall back to the bundled webpki roots when no certificates load from the OS trust store, as QUIC connections already did. They used to fail with `NativeCertsNotFound` before reaching the server
- `lore-server`: `[server.quic_internal]` sizes the flow-control windows of every connection it accepts for a 220 ms round trip, up from 100 ms. Replication connections to `OtherRegion` peers use the same value. A peer in a distant region can keep more than twice as much data in flight. Set the endpoint's value with `transport_rtt`
- `RelativePath` keeps its view offsets in 32 bits, 24 bytes inline rather than 40. On a 5-million-change sync this lowers the memory held after the diff from 2.9 to 2.7 GiB and the peak resident size from 3.9 to 3.8 GB
- `lore repository instance prune` keeps an instance whose instance file cannot be read on filesystems that report an empty directory's size as zero, such as Btrfs: reading a directory as a file fails instead of reading as empty
- `lore-server`: repository create and delete return `INVALID_ARGUMENT` for the all-zero repository id. This id identifies the namespace-root partition holding the repository name table
- `lore-revision`: links and layers name both sides of a mount the same way, `mount_path` and `source_path`. No behaviour change
- `lore-server` times each branch push in five phases: prepare, verify, fast-forward merge, commit and respond (`lore.branch_push.phase_duration`). A push dropped before it returns, such as by the handler timeout or a server shutting down, counts the phase it was in (`lore.branch_push.cancelled_phase`). Fragment verification also times its tree walk and existence checks (`lore.branch_push.verify_collect_duration`, `lore.branch_push.verify_exist_duration`). Each push also records its compare-and-swap attempts to store the new head (`lore.branch_push.store_latest_attempts`) and the size of its fast-forward merge (`lore.branch_push.fast_forward_merge_changes`), and logs the breakdown of a push that is cut off, fails or takes 10s or more at info
- A revision named by number, such as `<branch>@<number>`, resolves from the first page the remote returns for it, rather than walking the branch's history back from its latest revision one page at a time
- Following a branch's history through the remote no longer takes the revisions a page holds above the one it was asked for as that revision's ancestors. A page the server serves from a cached segment holds them, and finding the revision two branches share could answer with one of them, newer than the one they really share
- On Windows, a Lore service started while another serves the same socket exits without serving, as it does on Linux and macOS. It used to take the socket over and leave the first service running unreachable, holding its SWFS mounts until killed, so commands that each started a service at the same moment could leave one behind per extra command
- A branch push reads each mutable store key once, loads the branch alongside the pushed revision, and checks the branch name while it verifies the revision's fragments rather than before, so a push spends fewer store round trips before it moves the branch. A push the server refuses because the branch is protected no longer reinstates the name of a deleted branch first
- T

entries.title: lore\release-notes\README.md
entries.text:
Add a note for every change to what Lore does, for anyone who runs the client, operates a server,
or builds on its API or data. That includes changes that aren't visible on the command line:
server behaviour, authentication and authorization, replication and storage, the protocol, the
revision data structures such as the merkle tree, performance and resource use, logging and
telemetry, and configuration. A refactor counts when it changes observable behaviour, timing,
errors or resource use.

Skip the note only when the change touches nothing that ships: tests, CI, build scripts and
developer tooling, documentation other than release notes, formatting, or a refactor that leaves
behaviour, output and stored data exactly as they were.

entries.title: lore\release-notes\README.md
entries.text:
Copy [`_template.md`](_template.md) to `docs/release-notes/<summary>.md`:

- Name it after what changed, in a few lowercase words joined by hyphens, such as
  `sync-keeps-view-escapes.md`. Don't name it after a branch, a ticket or a person.
- Set `type`. The release puts the note under the matching heading.
- Write the bullets as they should read in the release notes, each as
  `` - `code-area`: description ``, where the code area is the crate or component that changed,
  such as `lore-server`. Continuation
  lines are indented by two spaces, and there are no blank lines between bullets. Remove the
  template's comments.
- Describe the effect that a user, an operator or an integrator sees: the command, the behaviour,
  the result. Leave out crate-internal functions and types, byte sizes and mechanics.

Later work on the same change edits the same note.

entries.title: lore\roadmap.md
entries.text:
| Theme | Timeline | Status |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [**Lore OSS and UEFN compatibility**](#lore-oss-and-uefn-compatibility) | 2026 | In progress |
| [**VS Code plugin**](#vs-code-plugin) | 2026 | In progress |
| [**Scalable file locking**](#scalable-file-locking) | 2026 | In progress |
| [**Virtual file system (VFS)**](#virtual-file-system) | 2026 | In progress |
| [**Links and layers**](#links-and-layers) | 2026 | In progress |
| [**Desktop client**](#desktop-client) | 2027 | In progress |
| [**Unreal Editor plugin**](#unreal-editor-plugin) | 2027 | In progress |
| [**Web client**](#web-client) | 2027 | Committed |
| [**Edge instances and advanced server topologies**](#edge-instances-and-advanced-server-topologies) | 2027 | Exploring |
| [**Forks and isolated partitions**](#forks-and-isolated-partitions) | Later | Exploring |

**Status legend**:

- **In progress** — actively underway, with the foundations already in place
- **Committed** — we've committed to delivering it, but the work hasn't started yet
- **Exploring** — we know we want it and are working out the shape

> [!NOTE]
> This roadmap is **directional, not a guarantee**. Timelines are targets, not commitments, and the order reflects today's thinking. As a 0.x project shaped in the open, priorities move in response to what the community builds, reports, and asks for — so expect this page to evolve. Want to influence it? See [Help shape the roadmap](#help-shape-the-roadmap).

entries.title: lore\roadmap.md
entries.text: The near-term focus is putting the foundations that team-wide, large-scale deployments depend on in place: locking that scales, workflows that stay fast on the largest repositories, finishing the multi-repository composition the data model already supports, and bringing Lore into the editor developers already work in.

entries.title: lore\roadmap.md
entries.text:
**Timeline:** 2026 · **Status:** In progress

**Converge the OSS and UEFN implementations of Lore so open-source clients, libraries, and SDKs can talk to UEFN's hosted Lore implementation directly.** Lore is the built-in version control system for UEFN (Unreal Editor for Fortnite), but today's open-source tooling can't talk to it: Lore uses the open-source Zstandard compression format, but UEFN projects use Oodle, which isn't compatible. We're actively moving UEFN onto Zstandard to eliminate the gap between the two.

entries.title: lore\roadmap.md
entries.text:
**Timeline:** 2026 · **Status:** In progress

**Bring a graphical Lore interface into Visual Studio Code, where everyday operations are a click away.** Everything in Lore is reachable through the CLI and API today; this plugin surfaces those operations visually, in an editor many developers already use — making version control discoverable instead of something you have to memorize. We intend to release both the plugin and its source code as a complementary repository as part of the overall Lore project.

entries.title: lore\roadmap.md
entries.text:
**Timeline:** 2026 · **Status:** In progress

**Scale locking so that it can enforce single-editor access across millions of files and thousands of concurrent users.** Lore has basic locking today — users can lock a non-mergeable asset to signal that it's being edited — but the current implementation informs rather than enforces, and lock state is queried globally across the repository, which doesn't scale. The next iteration focuses on enforcement and cross-branch lock scalability at that size, so lock state stays correct and cheap to query no matter how large the repository or team grows. Locking is the recommended workflow for binary assets where two people should never be editing at once, so making it scale is foundational for large art teams.

entries.title: lore\roadmap.md
entries.text:
**Timeline:** 2026 · **Status:** In progress

**Implement a virtual file system (VFS) so you can be productive in a multi-terabyte project moments after cloning — and never store it more than once.** Lore works sparsely today — a clone brings down only the part of the project you ask for — but you choose that part up front, and every branch or workstream you keep locally is another full copy on disk. By adding a virtual file system, Lore can load files lazily as you open them and serve them from Lore's existing [shared store](glossary.md#shared-store), extending Lore's fragment-level [deduplication](glossary.md#deduplication) and ensuring that content only lives on disk once. The larger a project grows and the more branches a team runs at once, the larger the cost of up-front clones, incremental syncs, and on-disk storage — so a VFS is foundational to keeping growing projects workable.

entries.title: lore\roadmap.md
entries.text:
**Timeline:** 2026 · **Status:** In progress

**Unlock composition of multiple repositories into a single working tree, with access scoped to each link.** Lore's data model already expresses multi-repository composition through [links](glossary.md#link) and [layers](glossary.md#layer): a link is a pinned reference to a subtree of another repository, recorded in the parent's revision so it travels with every clone, while a layer overlays one repository's content onto another at materialization time. Each linked repository is its own [partition](glossary.md#partition) with its own access control, which is how Lore expresses per-directory access policy — but today that capability lives in the data model rather than in a workflow you can reach for. We're finishing and exposing it as a first-class operation, so teams can easily assemble shared libraries and multiple repositories into one working tree while still ensuring that each contributor only sees the partitions they're entitled to.

entries.title: lore\roadmap.md
entries.text:
**Timeline:** 2027 · **Status:** In progress

**Surface a visual version-control workflow inside the Unreal Editor, the interface you already work in.** A Lore plugin brings everyday Lore operations directly into the tool artists and developers use to build with Unreal Engine, so versioning your work is a native part of the editor rather than a separate command-line step — and artists who never touch a terminal can manage it themselves. It builds on the Lore plugin that already ships with UEFN, and rather than living as a separate Lore project, it will be included in the native Unreal Engine codebase and delivered as part of the engine itself.

entries.title: lore\roadmap.md
entries.text:
**Timeline:** 2027 · **Status:** Committed

**Open-source the web client so teams get a shared, browser-based home for code review and repository management.** Provide a home where changes get reviewed and discussed before they land, and where teams manage their repositories day to day — all in the browser. Unlike a desktop binary, a web client is a little more complex to package in a form that any team can readily stand up and self-host. We're working through exactly that, so the web client can ship as source alongside the rest of Lore. Similar to the desktop client, it's important that the web client is also fully open, so the community is free to review, extend, and shape it.

entries.title: lore\roadmap.md
entries.text:
**Timeline:** 2027 · **Status:** Exploring

**Iterate and optimize Lore server replication to support even the most extreme use cases.** Lore already supports distributed teams through server replication across clustered servers and regions. This work is about the extreme cases where there's room to optimize how Lore replicates and caches so it stays fast no matter how far a project reaches. The more locations and regions a studio spans, the more its everyday speed depends on replication holding up under that load — so optimizing it is foundational for the largest, most distributed teams.

entries.title: lore\roadmap.md
entries.text:
**Timeline:** Later · **Status:** Exploring

**Add the ability to fork projects so that teams can experiment and take projects in unique directions, as an independent, access-controlled copy whose changes can always merge back into its source.** The data model already describes a [fork](glossary.md#fork) as a separate [partition](glossary.md#partition) with its own access control — it shares a source repository's initial content but evolves independently, filled in lazily through copy-on-write. But that capability lives in the data model rather than a workflow you can reach for. We intend to finish and expose forks as a first-class operation, so that separate teams can push shared projects forward without sharing write access — each working in their own access-controlled copy, each able to merge work back to the shared source.

entries.title: lore\roadmap.md
entries.text:
Lore is built in the open, and this roadmap reflects community input as much as our own plans. There are a few ways to weigh in:

- **Have an idea or a need?** Post in [`#feature-requests` on Discord](https://discord.gg/E4SFJKRPbg) or open a [GitHub Issue](https://github.com/EpicGames/lore/issues). Real-world use cases are what move items up this page.
- **Want to build one of these?** Many of these themes are great places to contribute. Read [CONTRIBUTING.md](https://github.com/EpicGames/lore/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) and look for the [`good-first-issue`](https://github.com/EpicGames/lore/labels/good-first-issue) label to get started.
- **Proposing a significant change?** Changes to the wire protocol, on-disk format, or public APIs go through a [Lore Enhancement Proposal](https://github.com/EpicGames/lore/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md#lore-enhancement-proposals) — the place where the biggest roadmap items get designed in public.

Governance of Lore is evolving toward a technical steering group drawn from both internal and external contributors, operating through public roadmaps, RFCs, and open meetings. This page is part of that commitment to deciding Lore's direction in the open.

entries.title: lore\tutorials\getting-started-with-lore-for-unreal-editor.md
entries.text:
Follow [Install the Lore CLI](../how-to/install-lore-cli.md), then the *Run from the binary* section of [Deploy a local Lore Server](../how-to/deploy-local-lore-server.md).

Keep the server's configuration file, certificate files, and store outside your Unreal Engine project. Add these settings to `config/local.toml`:

```toml
[server]
trust_unsigned_identity = true

[server.quic]
host = "127.0.0.1"

[server.grpc]
host = "127.0.0.1"

[server.http]
host = "127.0.0.1"
```

> [!WARNING]
> With `trust_unsigned_identity = true`, any caller can claim any identity. Binding every listener to `127.0.0.1` keeps other machines out, but any process on your computer can still connect. Use this setting only on a single-user development computer, never on a shared server. See [Unsigned identity](../reference/lore-server-config.md#unsigned-identity).

These settings accept the identity names supplied by clients and keep the server accessible only on your computer. Start the server with that configuration and keep it running while you use the editor.

Check the server's health endpoint with an HTTP client of your choice:

```text
http://127.0.0.1:41339/health_check
```

Expect `HTTP/1.1 200 OK` with an empty body.

entries.title: lore\tutorials\getting-started-with-lore-for-unreal-editor.md
entries.text:
Use the Lore CLI to create the repository from the project folder containing the `.uproject` file:

```bash
lore --identity alice repository create lore://127.0.0.1:41337/MyProject
```

Replace `alice` with your name and `MyProject` with your project name. Lore creates a `.lore` directory beside the `.uproject` file.

Check that `.lore/config.toml` contains your identity. Keep the remote URL generated by Lore:

```toml
identity = "alice"
```

This tutorial uses a server on your own computer. To clone an existing remote repository, use `lore clone` instead of creating a new one.

entries.title: lore\tutorials\getting-started-with-lore-for-unreal-editor.md
entries.text:
Create an [ignore file](../glossary.md#ignore-file) named `.loreignore` in the project folder, beside `.uproject` and `.lore`. Make sure the filename doesn't end in `.txt`.

Use this starting point for Unreal Engine project files:

```gitignore
# Ignore everything, then include project files.
*
!*/
!/Content/**/*.uasset
!/Content/**/*.umap
!/Config/**/*.ini
!/Source/**
!*.verse
!*.uproject
!.loreignore

# Exclude generated folders.
/Binaries/
/DerivedDataCache/
/Intermediate/
/Saved/
```

Add rules for any project plugins or other files your project needs. When you review the submission in the editor, check that required files are included and generated files are excluded.

From the project folder, record the initial project files with the Lore CLI:

```bash
lore stage --scan .
lore status
```

Review the staged files. Include `.loreignore`, `.uproject`, and any required `Source/` or plugin files, then commit and push:

```bash
lore commit "Initial project revision"
lore push
```

The editor's submission flow covers assets, configuration, and the project file. Use the Lore CLI for project files outside those locations.

entries.title: lore\tutorials\getting-started-with-lore-for-unreal-editor.md
entries.text:
Open the project in Unreal Editor:

1. Open **Revision Control** in the bottom-right corner.
2. Select **Connect to Revision Control…**.
3. Set **Provider** to **Lore**.
4. Review the settings and click **Accept Settings**.

The editor connects to the repository containing your initial project revision.

entries.title: lore\tutorials\getting-started-with-lore-for-unreal-editor.md
entries.text:
Create your first revisions with a test asset:

1. Create a **Material** named `M_LoreTest` in the **Content Browser**.
2. Save the material.
3. Click **Check In Changes**. Review the files and submit with the description `Add test material`.
4. Check out the material from its **Revision Control** menu and open it.
5. Enable **Two Sided** in the **Details** panel and save the material.
6. Click **Check In Changes**. Review the files and submit with the description `Update test material`.
7. Open **Branch History** and find both revisions.

Now that you've created your first Lore revisions in Unreal Editor, you're ready to keep building your project while leveraging all of the Lore plugin's features.

This tutorial doesn't cover every feature, but be sure to explore:

- Optional settings in **Editor Preferences** to check out assets automatically when you modify them and to back up work automatically on save
- Creating and managing branches with the **Branch Explorer**
- Comparing changes, resolving conflicts, restoring earlier revisions, and more

entries.title: lore\tutorials\getting-started-with-lore-for-unreal-editor.md
entries.text:
In addition to its in-editor UI, the Lore plugin also exposes commands through the Unreal MCP, enabling you to:

- Check the connection and repository status
- Inspect file states and pending assets
- Check out files and mark files for addition or deletion
- Validate and submit pending changes
- Browse revision history and submission details
- Load historical asset versions or download file revisions
- Sync revisions and revert local changes
- List, create, switch, push, merge, delete, and restore branches
- Resolve conflicts and restore an earlier revision as the latest revision

Now try it out. With your agent connected to Unreal Editor's Model Context Protocol (MCP) server, ask:

> Check that Lore is connected, then show the status and revision history of my test asset. Use the asset's full file path.

Check out `M_LoreTest` and make another edit, such as disabling **Two Sided**. Save the material in the editor before asking your agent to validate and submit it.

MCP submission includes all files eligible for check-in through the editor. Review all pending changes before submitting. After submitting, ask your agent to check the asset's status and history again.

After submitting, the editor reports **All Saved** and **At Latest**.

entries.title: lore\tutorials\quickstart.md
entries.text:
Run Lore's install script in demo mode. It downloads the prebuilt `lore` CLI and `loreserver` binaries, puts them on your PATH, and starts a local server. With no configuration, the server starts a single-node instance, generating an ephemeral self-signed certificate and a temporary store under your system temporary directory.

<!-- tabs:start -->

<!-- tab -->
**macOS / Linux**

```bash
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/EpicGames/lore/main/scripts/install.sh | bash -s -- --demo
```

<!-- tab -->
**Windows**

```powershell
$env:LORE_DEMO=1; irm https://raw.githubusercontent.com/EpicGames/lore/main/scripts/install.ps1 | iex
```

<!-- tabs:end -->

The server keeps running in this terminal, listening on port 41337 for QUIC and gRPC and on port 41339 for HTTP. Open a new terminal for the rest of the tutorial, and leave this one alone — pressing Ctrl-C or closing it stops the server.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> Run with no config, the server generates an ephemeral self-signed certificate and a store under your system temporary directory (`<temp>/lore-server`). The certificate is untrusted and regenerated on every restart, and the temporary store isn't durable across reboots — both are fine for a throwaway tutorial server. To deploy a more persistent Lore server see [Deploy a local Lore Server](../how-to/deploy-local-lore-server.md) and for the full list of server configurables, see the [Lore Server config reference](../reference/lore-server-config.md#zero-config-defaults).

<!-- -->

> [!NOTE]
> Prefer a manual binary download, a custom PATH, or a build from source? See [Install the Lore CLI](../how-to/install-lore-cli.md).

entries.title: lore\tutorials\quickstart.md
entries.text:
In your new terminal, first confirm the server is healthy:

<!-- tabs:start -->

<!-- tab -->
**macOS / Linux**

```bash
curl -i http://127.0.0.1:41339/health_check
```

<!-- tab -->
**Windows**

```powershell
curl.exe -i http://127.0.0.1:41339/health_check
```

<!-- tabs:end -->

A healthy server returns `HTTP/1.1 200 OK` with an empty body. The server starts with auth disabled — no credentials are needed for this tutorial.

Now create a repository:

<!-- tabs:start -->

<!-- tab -->
**macOS / Linux**

```bash
mkdir ~/my-project && cd ~/my-project
```

<!-- tab -->
**Windows**

```powershell
mkdir ~/my-project
cd ~/my-project
```

<!-- tabs:end -->

```bash
lore repository create lore://127.0.0.1:41337/my-project
```

Expected output:

```text
Created repository my-project in /home/you/my-project with ID 3f2a1b4c5d6e7f8a...
```

(Your path and ID will differ. The ID is a 32-character hex string.)

Lore initializes the repository on the server and creates a working tree in the current directory. A `.lore/` directory appears alongside your files — that's where Lore keeps its local state. Inside `.lore/` is the client config, `.lore/config.toml` — the remote URL, your commit identity, and local store settings. See the [Lore CLI configuration reference](../reference/lore-cli-config.md#per-repository-configtoml) for what's recorded there.

entries.title: lore\tutorials\quickstart.md
entries.text:
Create a text file:

```bash
echo "Hello, Lore" > hello.txt
```

Create a small binary file:

<!-- tabs:start -->

<!-- tab -->
**macOS / Linux**

```bash
python3 -c "import os; open('sample.bin', 'wb').write(os.urandom(256))"
```

<!-- tab -->
**Windows**

```powershell
fsutil file createnew sample.bin 256
```

<!-- tabs:end -->

Stage both files:

```bash
lore stage hello.txt sample.bin
```

Confirm the staged state:

```bash
lore status --scan
```

Expected output (no revisions yet, so the revision number is 0 and its hash is all zeros):

```text
Repository 3f2a1b4c5d6e7f8a...
On branch main revision 0 -> 0000000000000000...
Remote revision 0 -> 0000000000000000...
Local branch in sync with remote
Changes staged for commit:
A hello.txt
A sample.bin
```

(Your repository ID will differ. The `A` prefix means the file is newly added.)

> [!NOTE]
> `lore stage` covers adds, edits, and deletes — you use the same command for all three. Stage a deleted file and Lore records the deletion for the next commit. Moves and renames are tracked too, through a dedicated subcommand: `lore stage move <from> <to>` records the rename so the file keeps its identity and history across the move instead of registering as a delete plus an add.

entries.title: lore\tutorials\quickstart.md
entries.text:
Record the staged files as a new revision:

```bash
lore commit "Initial revision"
```

Expected output:

```text
Fragmenting files and updating tree hashes
Committing staged changes
Committed 1/1 directories, 2/2 files, 269.00 bytes/269.00 bytes (2 modified, 0 deleted)
Repository: 3f2a1b4c5d6e7f8a...
Revision  : 1
Signature : a3f8c2d1...
Branch    : e7263180...
Date      : Wed, 14 Jan 2026 09:24:18 +0000
    Initial revision
Commit succeeded
```

(Your repository ID, hashes, and timestamp will differ.)

The revision is local until you push it. Staging and committing work fully offline — no server round-trip is needed for either step.

> [!NOTE]
> An unauthenticated server like this one won't record a commit author, but you can still keep a who-did-what history by setting your own identity. You can choose to set your identity in `.lore/config.toml` (seeded for you when you pass `--identity you@google.com` to `lore repository create` or `lore clone`), to ensure commits are attributed to you from then on. The demo skips this, so its commits record no author — fine for a throwaway run. See the [CLI configuration reference](../reference/lore-cli-config.md#identity) for more info.

entries.title: lore\tutorials\quickstart.md
entries.text:
Upload the revision to the server:

```bash
lore push
```

Expected output:

```text
Pushing 1 fragment(s)
Pushed 1 fragment(s), 124.00 bytes
Pushing a3f8c2d1... to branch main
Pushed revision 1 -> a3f8c2d1... to branch main
```

(Your hashes and byte count will differ — the byte count is the size of the stored, compressed fragments, not the size of your files.)

> [!CAUTION]
> If `lore push` fails with a conflict error, another client pushed to the same branch since your last sync. Run `lore sync` to pull the remote changes, resolve any conflicts, commit the merge, then push again.

entries.title: lore\tutorials\quickstart.md
entries.text:
Now that the repository has a revision on the server, clone it into a sibling directory to get a second, independent working tree, and keep that tree's content in a *shared store*. With a shared store, you can keep multiple working trees on your machine without each one costing its own disk space: instead of copying content into every tree's `.lore/`, all the trees that point at the store draw from one on-disk copy. Any tree cloned from the same server can use it, and because Lore stores content as deduplicated *fragments*, even similar files share the parts they have in common — not just byte-for-byte duplicates.

Clone into the sibling directory, adding `--use-shared-store` so the new tree keeps its content in the shared store instead of its own `.lore/`. There's no store for this server yet, so the clone creates one first:

```bash
cd ~
lore clone lore://127.0.0.1:41337/my-project my-project-b --use-shared-store
```

Expected output:

```text
[Warn] Creating new shared store for remote lore://127.0.0.1:41337 in shared store at /home/you/.local/share/lore/shared_store/127.0.0.1_41337/shared_store
Cloning repository 3f2a1b4c5d6e7f8a... branch main into /home/you/my-project-b
Pull state a3f8c2d1...
Cloned 2/2 files (269.00 bytes/269.00 bytes)
Branch main revision a3f8c2d1...
Clone complete in 0.12s
```

(Your repository ID, hashes, timing, and store path will differ. The store lives in Lore's data directory, shown here for Linux.)

The clone already contains the committed files — confirm it:

<!-- tabs:start -->

<!-- tab -->
**macOS / Linux**

```bash
cd ~/my-project-b && lore status && ls
```

<!-- tab -->
**Windows**

```powershell
cd ~/my-project-b
lore status
ls
```

<!-- tabs:end -->

```text
Repository 3f2a1b4c5d6e7f8a...
On branch main revision 1 -> a3f8c2d1...
Remote revision 1 -> a3f8c2d1...
Local branch in sync with remote
hello.txt
sample.bin
```

You now have two independent working trees of the same repository.

To have every later `lore clone` and `lore repository create` on this machine use the shared store without the flag, turn on automatic use:

```bash
lore shared-store set-use-automatically true
```

`lore shared-store info` shows the setting and where the store lives:

```text
Shared store will be used automatically: true
Remote URL: 127.0.0.1:41337
  Path: /home/you/.local/share/lore/shared_store/127.0.0.1_41337/shared_store
  Exists: true
```

`~/my-project`, created in Step 2 before the store existed, keeps its own store in `.lore/`. Only working trees cloned over the shared store draw from it.

> [!TIP]
> Working trees over a shared store are Lore's equivalent of worktrees, with no main repository. To keep one for each branch, build, or automated tool, and to list, move, prune, and remove them, see [Run parallel instances over a shared store](../how-to/run-parallel-instances-over-a-shared-store.md).

Go back into the first working tree:

```bash
cd ~/my-project
```

> [!CAUTION]
> If a step fails with a connection error, check that the server is still running: `curl -i http://127.0.0.1:41339/health_check` (`curl.exe` on Windows). If it's not responding, restart the `loreserver` process by re-running the install command from Step 1, then check the health endpoint again.

entries.title: lore\tutorials\quickstart.md
entries.text:
Create a branch from the current revision and switch your working tree to it:

```bash
lore branch create my-first-branch
```

Expected output:

```text
Created branch my-first-branch at revision a3f8c2d1...
```

Add a file on the branch, then stage and commit it:

```bash
echo "Notes added on a branch." > notes.txt
lore stage notes.txt
lore commit "Add notes on a branch"
```

Expected output:

```text
Fragmenting files and updating tree hashes
Committing staged changes
Committed 1/1 directories, 1/1 files, 25.00 bytes/25.00 bytes (1 modified, 0 deleted)
Stored history for 2 nodes
Repository: 3f2a1b4c5d6e7f8a...
Revision  : 2
Signature : b4e9f0a2...
Parent    : a3f8c2d1...
Branch    : 9a1c4b7d...
Date      : Wed, 14 Jan 2026 09:26:02 +0000
    Add notes on a branch
Commit succeeded
```

The branch now has a revision (2) that `main` doesn't. The `Parent` line points back at the revision you branched from.

entries.title: lore\tutorials\quickstart.md
entries.text:
Switch back to `main`. Lore updates your working tree to match `main`, so `notes.txt` disappears for now — it lives only on the `my-first-branch` branch until you merge it.

```bash
lore branch switch main
```

```text
Switching branch to main, using current remote latest revision a3f8c2d1...
Calculating deltas 2 -> 1
Verifying 1 changes with local file system
Switched to branch main revision a3f8c2d1...
```

Merge the branch into the current branch (`main`). `lore branch merge` takes the **source** branch as its argument:

```bash
lore branch merge my-first-branch --message "Merge my-first-branch into main"
```

Lore prints the diff it computes between the branches (omitted as `...` below), then the merge result. A clean merge with no conflicts commits a new revision automatically:

```text
Starting merge of branch 9a1c4b7d... revision b4e9f0a2...
...
Merged files, 1 updated, 0 deleted, 0 merged, 0 conflicted
Staged merged repository state 5e2a9f10...
Fragmenting files and updating tree hashes
Stored history for 3 nodes
Committed merged repository state 3 -> c7d1e8b3...
```

`main` is now at revision 3, with `notes.txt` merged in — but that revision is local. Check the status and push it to the server:

```bash
lore status
lore push
```

```text
Repository 3f2a1b4c5d6e7f8a...
On branch main revision 3 -> c7d1e8b3...
Remote revision 1 -> a3f8c2d1...
Local branch is ahead of remote
Local branch is 1 revision(s) ahead of remote, pushing all revisions
Repository 3f2a1b4c5d6e7f8a...
Pushing 6 fragment(s)
Pushed 6 fragment(s), 603.00 bytes
Pushing c7d1e8b3... to branch main
Pushed revision 3 -> c7d1e8b3... to branch main
```

(Your hashes, fragment count, and byte count will differ.)

> [!NOTE]
> If the merge reports conflicts instead, Lore stages the merge and lists the conflicted files rather than committing. Resolve them with `lore branch merge resolve`, then commit — or run `lore branch merge abort` to back out.

entries.title: lore\tutorials\quickstart.md
entries.text:
Switch to the clone you made in Step 6 and pull the merged revision from the server:

```bash
cd ~/my-project-b
lore sync
```

Expected output:

```text
Sync from remote lore://127.0.0.1:41337
On branch main revision 1 -> a3f8c2d1...
Synchronizing to revision 3 -> c7d1e8b3...
Calculating deltas 1 -> 3
Verifying 1 changes with local file system
```

Confirm the merged file arrived:

```bash
ls
```

```text
hello.txt
notes.txt
sample.bin
```

`notes.txt` — created on a branch in one working tree, merged into `main`, pushed, and synced into the other working tree — completes the loop.

entries.title: lore\tutorials\run-commands-through-the-service.md
entries.text:
A command that the setting sends to the service starts one only from an executable you name, so the build serving your machine is one you chose. Name it once, with the absolute path of the `lore` you want serving your commands.

<!-- tabs:start -->

<!-- tab -->
**macOS / Linux**

```bash
lore service set-executable /usr/local/bin/lore
```

```text
Lore service executable set to /usr/local/bin/lore
```

<!-- tab -->
**Windows**

```powershell
lore service set-executable 'C:\Program Files\Lore\lore.exe'
```

```text
Lore service executable set to C:\Program Files\Lore\lore.exe
```

<!-- tabs:end -->

entries.title: lore\tutorials\run-commands-through-the-service.md
entries.text:
```bash
lore service set-use-automatically true
```

```text
Lore commands will be carried out by the service
```

Both settings are needed. With the setting on and no executable named, commands go to a service that's already running and fail with exit code 32 when none is, and Lore warns you of that when you turn the setting on.

entries.title: lore\tutorials\run-commands-through-the-service.md
entries.text:
Nothing is listening yet, so this starts a service and runs there. Use any repository path you have.

```bash
lore --repository ~/my-project status
```

The command behaves exactly as it did before. What changed is where it ran: the service that started here outlives the command and serves the next one too.

entries.title: lore\tutorials\run-commands-through-the-service.md
entries.text:
`lore service status` reports on the service without changing it. It names the build that is serving the machine, how long that service has been up, how many clients are connected to it, and how many SWFS mounts it holds. With nothing running it says so and still succeeds, so a script can branch on the output rather than on a connection failing.

```bash
lore service status
```

```text
Lore service is running
  Executable: /usr/local/bin/lore
  Uptime: 1h 4m 12s
  Connections: 1
  SWFS mounts: 0
```

The command counts its own connection, so a service nothing else is talking to reports one.

Trouble the service ran into while no command was running is buffered and printed under the status that reports it: failures while it was initializing, failures in the loop that accepts connections, and errors raised by SWFS callbacks. A service that has hit none of those reports none, so a status with no messages under it is the healthy reading rather than a missing one.

The buffer holds the most recent messages and is emptied as it is read, so each call shows what has arrived since the last one, and a call that finds messages were dropped says how many. These messages are the answer to the command that asked for them rather than diagnostics about it, so they are printed whatever `--log-level` is set to.

entries.title: lore\tutorials\run-commands-through-the-service.md
entries.text:
`LORE_USE_SERVICE` decides one command without changing the stored setting. It reads `0`, `false`, `no` and `off` as off.

<!-- tabs:start -->

<!-- tab -->
**macOS / Linux**

```bash
LORE_USE_SERVICE=0 lore --repository ~/my-project status
```

<!-- tab -->
**Windows**

PowerShell has no per-command environment prefix, so set the variable in a child process. Setting it in your own session would overwrite an override you had already set there, and clearing it afterwards would not put that back.

```powershell
powershell -NoProfile -Command '$env:LORE_USE_SERVICE = "0"; lore --repository ~/my-project status'
```

<!-- tabs:end -->

> [!NOTE]
> `lore service run` is the service rather than a client of one, so it always does the work itself whatever these settings say. Use it to run a service in the foreground and watch its output; Ctrl+C stops it cleanly and releases its socket, as `lore service stop` does.

entries.title: lore\tutorials\run-commands-through-the-service.md
entries.text:
```text
[Warn] No service executable is set. Commands will use a service that is already running, but will fail if none is running. To let commands start a service when needed, set an executable with `lore service set-executable <path>`, or under [service] executable in the global config.
```

You turned the service on without naming an executable. Commands go to a service that's already running, and fail with exit code 32 when none is. Run `lore service set-executable <path>` so that they start one when needed.

entries.title: lore\tutorials\run-commands-through-the-service.md
entries.text:
```text
[Error] Failed to send command to Lore service because: Lore service unavailable:
starting /opt/lore/bin/lore failed: No such file or directory (os error 2)
```

The command never ran, because no service could be reached and none could be started from the executable that is named. Check that the path in `[service] executable` still exists — this is what you see after a build directory is cleaned or a version is uninstalled. Exit code `32` means the service was unreachable, distinct from the command itself having run and failed, so a script can retry it after starting a service.

entries.title: lore\tutorials\run-commands-through-the-service.md
entries.text: A build directory that is still on the machine keeps serving commands after you have moved on to another one, because the executable is resolved from the stored setting rather than from the client you ran. `lore service status` names the build that is actually serving the socket, so compare its `Executable` against the client you meant to use and re-run `lore service set-executable <path>` followed by `lore service stop` if they differ. The next command starts a service from the newly named build.

entries.title: lore\tutorials\run-commands-through-the-service.md
entries.text:
Every service belonging to a user answers on the same socket by default, which is what makes one service serve every command you run. Set `LORE_SERVICE_SOCKET` to give a group of processes a service of their own:

<!-- tabs:start -->

<!-- tab -->
**macOS / Linux**

```bash
export LORE_SERVICE_SOCKET=lore_service-my-checkout
```

<!-- tab -->
**Windows**

```powershell
$env:LORE_SERVICE_SOCKET = 'lore_service-my-checkout'
```

<!-- tabs:end -->

The value names a single file, not a path. Lore refuses anything containing a path separator and uses the default instead.

entries.title: lore\tutorials\work-in-a-virtual-clone.md
entries.text:
```text
[Error] Lore service unavailable: A FUSE clone is mounted by the Lore service, and no service could be reached or started: starting /opt/lore/bin/lore failed: No such file or directory (os error 2)
```

No service was running, and none could be started from the executable named for it, with `lore service set-executable` or in `LORE_SERVICE_EXECUTABLE`, so nothing was created. Name one that exists, or clear the setting with `lore service set-executable ""` and unset `LORE_SERVICE_EXECUTABLE` to have the clone start the service from the `lore` you run, then clone again.

entries.title: lore\tutorials\work-in-a-virtual-clone.md
entries.text:
```text
[Error] Repository not found: /home/you/my-project-fuse
```

No service is running, so the clone isn't mounted and its directory is empty, for example after `lore service stop` or a restart. Run `lore service start`: it mounts every virtual clone it finds again, with your uncommitted changes in place.

entries.title: lore\tutorials\work-in-a-virtual-clone.md
entries.text:
```text
[Error] File has local changes: hello.txt (incoming size 18 bytes, file system size 14 bytes)
[Error] Local modifications prevent synchronization
```

`lore sync` or `lore branch switch` would replace a file you changed but haven't committed, so it stops before changing anything. Commit the change, throw it away with `lore reset <path>`, or run the command again with `--force` to take the incoming version.

entries.title: lore\tutorials\work-in-a-virtual-clone.md
entries.text:
```text
[Error] Mounts are busy: /home/you/my-project-fuse
```

A shell or a program has its working directory or an open file inside a virtual clone. Leave the clone and close the program, then stop again. `lore service stop --force` detaches every mount at once instead, and the programs inside a detached clone lose access to it.

entries.title: lore\tutorials\work-in-a-virtual-clone.md
entries.text: The service that served the clone stopped without taking its mount down, for example after a crash. Run `lore service start`: it detaches the dead mount and mounts every virtual clone it can reach again. Deletions are recorded without syncing to disk, so a crash can bring back a file you deleted just before it.

entries.title: net\NETWORK-STACK.md
entries.text:
| Phase | `net probe` (prd, rustls 0.23.46 ring, platform verifier) | Chrome 157 (PC, owner profile, Navigation Timing) |
|---|---|---|
| DNS | 2.0 ms (system resolver, 8 AAAA + 8 A) | 0 (connection reused) |
| Connect | 1.3 ms (IPv6 first) | 0 (reused) |
| TLS | 7.7 ms, TLSv1_3, TLS13_AES_256_GCM_SHA384, chain 3 | 0 (reused) |
| TTFB | 114 ms, HTTP 200, `server: ESF` | 245 ms |
| Protocol | ALPN h2; Alt-Svc advertises `h3=":443"` and `h3-29` | `nextHopProtocol` h3, 65 h3 resources |
| Auth | n/a (no cookies, by design) | avatar and prompt box present |

Gap 1: we stop at h2; Chrome is already on h3 (QUIC). Gap 2: our cipher choice comes from rustls defaults, not Chromium's order (Chromium/BoringSSL prefers AES-128-GCM when AES-NI is available; to verify in //net and BoringSSL sources).

entries.title: net\NETWORK-STACK.md
entries.text:
| Layer | Today in src (rg) | Target | Gaps |
|---|---|---|---|
| Kernel Windows 11 (AFD, WFP, TCPIP) | nothing explicit; std/tokio sockets | keep the defaults; expose TCP Fast Open and the `SIO_*` timestamps only where measured | Windows networking docs on MS Learn not checked yet (to verify) |
| Kernel Linux (prd, fr1, fr2) | nothing explicit | BBR, io_uring for servers, kTLS for nginx/static | prd kernel version, congestion control and kTLS support not checked (to verify: `sysctl net.ipv4.tcp_congestion_control`) |
| bun runtime | `fetch`, `Bun.serve`, `WebSocket` across packages/* | keep it for app code; use `@aphrody/net` for diagnostics | bun exposes no per-phase timings or ALPN; bridged through bun:ffi (`packages/net`) |
| Rust | rustls/tokio-rustls in apps/rosegriffon (aphrody-nie-net), apps/shenron, crates/up; no hickory and no quinn in the root lock | `crates/net`: hickory (DoH/DoT), rustls + platform verifier, hyper/h2, h3 + quinn, tokio-tungstenite | one TLS config per app today; no shared verifier and no ALPN or cipher policy |
| Chromium //net | upstream Chrome 157 on the PC | the fork's `//net` = the reference behaviour (QUIC, DoH, ECH) | no NetLog export captured yet; CDP `Network.responseReceived.timing` is used instead |
| Servers | Bun.serve, nginx on fr2 (CDN), Workers | h3 everywhere at the edge | h3 on fr2 nginx not checked (to verify) |
| Clients | fetch, chromium-bun CDP (`packages/chromium-bun/src/browser/cdp-client.ts`), agent-browser, CLI | every client reports the same `Trace` | |

entries.title: packaging\RECOMMENDATION.md
entries.text:
Principe : étendre `crates/up`, ne rien réécrire.

1. Lock unique `src.lock.json` v2 : chaque entrée = `purl` + version + digest sha256/OCI + provenance (attestation) ; `tools.toml` devient la déclaration (intentions), le lock la résolution.
2. Trait `Backend` dans crates/up : `resolve(spec) -> Locked`, `fetch(Locked) -> Path`, `verify`. Backends :
   - existants : `github`, `url`, `bun`, `installer`, `ubi` (à doter d'un checksum calculé au lock, stocké dans le lock) ;
   - `cipd` (crates/depot-cipd), `uv` (crates/depot-vpython), `winget` (packages/machine DSC, export -> lock) ;
   - nouveaux : `oci` (oci-client 0.18 + oci-spec 0.10 : images et artefacts ORAS, distribution de nos binaires via registre), `conda` (rattler 0.55 + resolvo 0.12) pour outils natifs multi-OS, `pacman` (alpm 5.0) côté prd, `apt` piloté en CLI côté fr1/fr2.
3. Stockage : `depot-cas` comme cache content-addressed partagé (dédup FastCDC), servi depuis R2.
4. Sécurité : vérif GitHub attestations/sigstore quand publiées ; requête OSV par purl au `ay lock`.
5. Solveur : resolvo seulement pour les backends à dépendances (conda) ; les outils restent épinglés.

entries.text:
- `npm whoami` en local renvoie **401** : le token de `~/.npmrc` est expiré ou révoqué. La propriété n'a donc pas pu être confirmée directement.
- Indices : `@aphrody/web` (1.4.7) et `@aphrody/yolo` (3.2.0) ont pour seul mainteneur `yohan971` (adresse @live.fr). `@aphrody/yolo` déclare `repository: aphrody-code/YOLO` et `author: aphrody-code`. Il s'agit très probablement du compte du propriétaire.
- À faire : `npm login`, puis `npm whoami` (doit répondre `yohan971`) et `npm org ls aphrody`.

entries.text:
Chromium (`libcef`, Blink C++, Skia C++, V8) imposes >120 MB binary overhead, multi-process IPC serialization bottlenecks, and C++ memory-safety liabilities. By fusing the 6 upstream Rust organizations with our local workspaces in `C:\src`, we achieve **two complementary, 100% Pure-Rust native rendering pipelines** sharing the exact same lower layers (`tokio` -> `wgpu`/`naga` -> `taffy` + `aphrody-design-tokens`):

1. **Path A — Web/HTML/CSS-Compatible Reactive DOM without Chromium (`Dioxus 0.8` + `Blitz` + `Stylo` + `Taffy` + `Parley` + `Vello` + `WGPU`)**:
   - `dioxus` (`rsx!`, `dioxus-core`, `dioxus-signals`, `subsecond` hot-patching, `manganis` asset linker) drives a zero-JS VirtualDOM directly into `dioxus-native` / `blitz-dom`.
   - `servo/html5ever` parses HTML/SVG markup; `servo/stylo` + `selectors` + `cssparser` (or `lightningcss` in `crates/aphrody-design-layout`) resolves the CSS3/CSS4 cascade in parallel across CPU cores.
   - `stylo_taffy` translates computed styles into `DioxusLabs/taffy` (`v0.15.0`) Flexbox, CSS Grid, Block, and Float layout trees, calling `linebender/parley` (`v0.12.0`) + `fontique` + `skrifa` + `harfrust` for inline rich-text shaping and line-breaking.
   - `blitz-paint` emits 2D vector draw commands through `DioxusLabs/anyrender` (`v0.14.0`) into `linebender/vello` (`v0.11.0` GPU compute shaders or `vello_cpu`/`vello_gpu` `v0.3` sparse strips) + `kurbo` (`v0.13.1`) + `peniko` (`v0.6.1`), executed on hardware via `gfx-rs/wgpu` (`v30.0.1`) and `naga` (`v30.0.1`).
2. **Path B — Ultra-Low-Latency GPU Workbench & Desktop Shell (`Zed GPUI` / `gpui-fast` + `Longbridge gpui-component` + `Taffy`)**:
   - `longbridge/gpui-kit` (`gpui-component` `v0.9.1`, checked out at `C:\src\third_party\gpui-component`) provides **90+ Shadcn/ui-grade GPU-accelerated native widgets** (Dock, Resizable Panels, VirtualList, Data Table, Command Palette, Code Editor/Syntect, Diff Viewer, Charts/Plots, Sheet, Popover, Tooltip, Form, Questionnaire, Markdown Streamer) rendered directly via GPUI's custom blade/wgpu/Metal/DX12 shader pipeline and laid out by `taffy`.

| LAYER 6: NATIVE GPU WIDGETS, WORKBENCH DOCK & MULTI-PLATFORM SHELL (longbridge + zed)              |

|     -> 85+ modules / 90+ Shadcn-equivalent GPU widgets (Dock, Table, VirtualList, Chart, Editor)   |
|   * longbridge/gpui-fast v0.1.14 & gpui-pre v0.3.12 (Standalone Zed GPUI + incremental layout)     |
|   * longbridge/gpui-mobile (iOS Metal / Android Vulkan) + longbridge/nsh (Native Shell)            |
|   * longbridge/rust-i18n v4.2.0 + quickjs-jit + C:\src\crates\aphrody-design-* (8-preset themes)   |
+====================================================================================================+
                                                  ^
                                                  |
+====================================================================================================+
| LAYER 5: REACTIVE VDOM, FULLSTACK SSR, ASSET LINKER & LAYOUT ENGINE (DioxusLabs)                   |
|   * DioxusLabs/dioxus v0.8.0-alpha.3 (dioxus-core, rsx!, dioxus-signals, dioxus-stores,            |
|     subsecond hotpatching, manganis compile-time assets, dioxus-fullstack, dioxus-ssr, router)     |
|   * DioxusLabs/blitz v0.3.0-beta.4 (blitz-dom, blitz-html, blitz-paint, blitz-net, blitz-shell,    |

#### Architecture & Execution Pipeline (Zero Node.js / Zero PostCSS)
1. **Compile-Time Macro (`tw!`) & Source Scanner (`tailwindcss-oxide`)**:
   - In Rust crates (`.rs` files for Dioxus/GPUI/Masonry), the `tw!("flex items-center gap-4 p-6 bg-surface-container-high text-on-surface rounded-xl shadow-md hover:bg-primary/10")` proc-macro invokes [`aphrody_design_layout::tailwind::resolve_tailwind`](file:///C:/src/crates/aphrody-design-layout/src/tailwind.rs#L36-L52) at compile time (`const` evaluation).
   - For hybrid `.tsx`/`.mdx`/`.html` files, `tailwindcss-oxide` + `bun_glob` scans the repository at >1.2 GB/s, extracting candidate utility tokens.
2. **Multi-Backend Code Emission**:
   - **Target A — Taffy / Layout Tree (`taffy::Style`)**: `LayoutStyle::to_taffy_style()` converts spacing (`p-*`, `m-*`, `gap-*`), sizing (`w-*`, `h-*`, `min-*`, `max-*`, `size-*`), Flexbox (`flex-*`, `justify-*`, `items-*`), and Grid (`grid-cols-*`, `col-span-*`) directly into `taffy::Style` with zero CSS string parsing at runtime.
   - **Target B — GPUI (`gpui::Styled`) & Vello (`vello::Scene`)**: [`aphrody_design_emit::gpui_theme`](file:///C:/src/crates/aphrody-design-emit/src/gpui_theme.rs) maps semantic M3/Shadcn colors (`bg-primary`, `text-muted-foreground`, `border-outline-variant`), elevation shadows, and corner radii directly to `gpui::Hsla` / `peniko::Color` and `kurbo::RoundedRect`.
   - **Target C — Servo Stylo (`stylo`) & Blitz DOM**: Emits pre-interned `stylo::properties::PropertyDeclarationBlock` atoms for instant parallel cascade matching in `blitz-dom`.
   - **Target D — Web CSS Bundle (`bun_css`)**: Emits a single tree-shaken `@layer theme, base, components, utilities;` stylesheet processed by `bun_css` with native `oklch()` / `color-mix()` / `@starting-style` lowering.
3. **Runtime Class Merging (`tw_merge` / `tailwind_fuse`)**:
   - Integrates `tailwind-fuse` (from [`third_party/rust-ui`](file:///C:/src/third_party/rust-ui/Cargo.toml)) with [`aphrody_design_layout::tailwind`](file:///C:/src/crates/aphrody-design-layout/src/tailwind.rs) conflict groups so runtime dynamic overrides (`tw_merge!("px-4 py-2 bg-primary", user_class)`) resolve deterministically in ~180 nanoseconds.

entries.title: reviews\gemini-2026-11-12-targets.md
entries.text:
| Tier | Cible | Pipeline de compilation | Emplacement & Contraintes |
|---|---|---|---|
| T1 | Vulkan SPIR-V | `clang` HLSL/CL → backend `SPIRV` (`spirv1.6-unknown-vulkan1.3-<stage>`) | `llvm-project` `[P]` ; validation via `SPIRV-Tools` (externe/vendored) |
| T2 | OpenCL / Kernel SPIR-V | Backend `SPIRV` (`spirv64-unknown-unknown`) ou `SPIRV-LLVM-Translator` | `SPIRV` in-tree `[P]` ; Translator externe (Khronos) |
| T1 | WGSL / WebGPU | SPIR-V / WGSL ↔ WGSL / MSL / HLSL via Naga ou Tint | Vendored : `third_party/wgpu` (Naga) & `third_party/dawn` (Tint) ; analyse `tree-sitter-wgsl` |
| T1 | Metal (MSL / AIR) | SPIR-V / WGSL → MSL via Naga / Tint (ou `SPIRV-Cross` externe) ; `.metallib` via `xcrun metal` | Pas de backend AIR dans LLVM public ; SDK Apple requis pour AIR binaire |
| T2 | D3D12 DXIL | Production : DXC (`dxcompiler` + signature `dxil.dll`). Veille : backend LLVM expérimental `DirectX` (`dxil-pc-shadermodel6.x-<stage>`) | `DirectX` dans `llvm-project` (expérimental, non signé) ; `dxil.dll` propriétaire requis en retail |
| T1 | CUDA / PTX | Backend `NVPTX` (`nvptx64-nvidia-cuda`) ; Triton (MLIR) | `NVPTX` in-tree `[P]` ; requiert CUDA headers + `libdevice` + `ptxas` propriétaire (SASS) |
| T1 | AMDGPU (ROCm) | Backend `AMDGPU` (`amdgcn-amd-amdhsa`, `-mcpu=gfx*`) ; Triton (MLIR) | `AMDGPU` in-tree `[P]` ; requiert ROCm `device-libs` (ou `llvm-libc` GPU) |
| Réf | Drivers Mesa | `src/compiler/clc` (OpenCL C → SPIR-V) & `src/compiler/nir` | `third_party/mesa` `[P]` (référence uniquement) |

entries.title: shell\MATRIX.md
entries.text:
- `bun C:\src\packages\machine\src\apply-user.ts --check` : tout est ok. Points contrôlés : CLAUDE_CODE_GIT_BASH_PATH, CLAUDE_CODE_USE_POWERSHELL_TOOL=0, MCP agent-desktop et agent-browser, PATH (niubash présent, Git Bash absent), profil par défaut de WT = niubash élevé.
- `niubash -c -l` (invocation de Claude) : BASH_VERSION 5.3.20, 59 options `shopt -p`, git et rg venant de niubash (sans MSYS).
- Limite : cette session tourne encore sous l'ancien Git Bash (5.3.15, /usr/bin/bash), lancé avant la bascule. Le contrôle de bout en bout (Bash tool sous niubash, avec context7, GitHub MCP et Microsoft Learn MCP) se fait dans une **nouvelle session** Claude Code : `echo $BASH_VERSION` doit afficher 5.3.20, puis on appelle un outil de chacun des trois MCP.
- pwsh : remplacé pour Claude, puisque l'outil PowerShell est désactivé et que niubash prend la place. Les usages restants (CIM, registre, Authenticode) passent par windows-rs ou les binaires Rust de src.
- **Contrôle de bout en bout fait** (nouvelle session `claude -p`, 2026-11-12) : l'outil Bash répond `5.3.20(1)-release` avec git venant de niubash ; context7 resolve « bun » → `/oven-sh/bun` ; GitHub MCP get_me → `aphrody-dev` ; Microsoft Learn search « CreateProcessW » → « CreateProcessW function (processthreadsapi.h) ». La chaîne Claude Code → niubash → MCP fonctionne sans Git Bash, pwsh, MSYS ni WSL.
- **Démarrage mesuré** (hyperfine -N, 20 runs, `-c exit`, ce PC, 2026-11-12 ; données dans startup.json) : osh Windows 8,8 ± 0,8 ms ; brush 0.4.0 9,3 ± 0,8 ms ; niubash 1.5.0 18,4 ± 0,6 ms ; nushell 28,5 ± 0,8 ms. Ces mesures remplacent la colonne [NV] pour ces quatre shells.
- **Cas d'usage pwsh sans pwsh** : sous niubash, `reg.exe query … /v CurrentBuild` renvoie bien 28120. `sudo.exe` en mode Inline répond. Le registre et l'élévation n'ont donc pas besoin de pwsh. La syntaxe `sudo reg query HKU\…` a échoué (clé invalide, mauvais échappement), donc la vérification de l'élévation reste à refaire.
- **Remplacement de pwsh testé de bout en bout** (session neuve `claude -p`, uniquement l'outil Bash, 2026-11-12) : l'outil PowerShell est absent ; Bash 5.3.20 ; registre lu (CurrentBuild 28120, i7-13700F) ; tasklist (346 processus) ; écriture puis suppression élevées dans HKLM via `sudo.exe reg.exe add/delete` réussies, la clé de test a disparu ensuite. Note : l'agent a posé `MSYS_NO_PATHCONV=1` pour les options `/v` `/f`, alors que niubash appelé directement passe `/v` sans conversion. Comportement à figer dans shell-matrix.
- **brush main (aphrody-labs/brush e9d45efe, sync upstream 2026-11-12, contient le fix #1398 d220c79d)** : cross-compilé sur prd avec cargo-xwin 0.23.1 (clang-cl/lld, sans MinGW), installé dans `C:\Users\aphro\.local\share\brush-main\brush.exe`. `brush.exe -c -l 'echo ok'` → `ok` : l'invocation de Claude passe. shell-matrix : **31/34** (claude 9/9, posix 9/9, bash 11/12, windows 2/4), contre niubash 1.5.0 34/34. Échecs : `bash-procsub`, `win-cd-drive`, `win-cd-native`. Médiane 12,7 ms par cas, niubash 25,6 ms.

entries.title: shell\modern-shells.md
entries.text:
- nushell : `polars` plugin (DataFrames), `explore` TUI, `nu --mcp` serveur MCP (ajouté ~0.106, NV), `stor` (SQLite en mémoire), sortie `to nuon`.
- elvish : pipelines de valeurs + octets séparés, `-lsp`, web UI `elvish -web` retiré (NV), éditeur `navigation mode`.
- murex : pipes typés, `tread`/`try` avec gestion d'erreurs stderr, prévisualisation man inline (F1).
- fish 4.x : binaire autonome avec fonctions embarquées (4.x, NV), `abbr --function`, paste bracketed, sans dépendance ncurses.
- oils : `ysh` avec JSON8, `--tool syntax-tree`, `osh` exécute plus de bash réel que la plupart (spec tests publics).
- xonsh : mode Python ou subprocess détecté à l'analyse, `@$(cmd)`, `!()` CommandPipeline objet.
- Amber : génère du bash vérifiable ; utile pour scripts sous brush, sous réserve compat (NV).
- es : `%pipe`, `%create` hooks redéfinissables (spawning remplaçable en script).
- rc : syntaxe Plan 9 minimale ; pas de build Windows natif trouvé.

entries.title: shell\modern-shells.md
entries.text:
- Aucun de ces shells n'exécute le snapshot bash de Claude Code (fonctions, `shopt`, `export -p`) sauf oils OSH (non natif Windows).
- Structurés natifs Windows utilisables à côté : nushell, elvish, murex, xonsh. Aucun ne remplace brush comme `CLAUDE_CODE_GIT_BASH_PATH`.
- Amber est un générateur de bash, pas un shell ; compatible avec brush à valider.

entries.text:
| Fichier | Rôle |

| `cpp/win32/posix_compat.h` | force-inclus (`-FI`) : types, constantes, signaux, wait macros, stat/glob/fnmatch/regex/termios/pwd… ; macros `open/access/stat/chdir/getcwd/unlink/isatty/execve` vers versions qui traduisent les chemins |
